sessions.name: GRACE-FO Project Status
sessions.description: The meeting will open with a GRACE-FO Project Status session consisting of the technical status of the mission and the flight segment, future science operations plans, as well as information on the latest GRACE/GRACE-FO data releases from the Science Data System.

sessions.name: Analysis Techniques & Inter-comparisons
sessions.description: This session invites presentations about methods, algorithms, and results from GRACE/GRACE-FO data analysis and error assessments providing insights into spatio-temporal signal content including diverse methods of error reduction. We also invite discussions on inter-comparisons between various GRACE/GRACE-FO gravity field time-series and assessments of the significance of the differences and analysis of possible causes.

sessions.name: GRACE-C, NGGM, and Future Missions
sessions.description: This session is for discussion on the status of the GRACE-FO successor mission GRACE-C, as well as ESA’s NGGM mission and on the progress towards the realization, technology, simulation, and error analyses of future mission concepts. Also invited are papers dealing with methods for bridging data gaps such as, e.g., between GRACE and GRACE-FO.

sessions.name: The Mean Earth Gravity Field
sessions.description: Results on combination, analysis, and geodetic/geodynamic interpretation of complementary results from GRACE/GRACE-FO, GOCE, altimetry, and terrestrial gravity data for the next generation of mean Earth gravity fields are invited to be presented in this session.

sessions.name: Solid Earth Sciences
sessions.description: This session invites presentations about studies of glacial isostatic adjustment, the Earth's crustal structure, lithospheric and mantle properties, analyses of seismic events, etc., using information from long-term mean and time-variable gravity field models.

sessions.name: Cryosphere
sessions.description: This session addresses changes of the Earth's ice sheets at all spatio-temporal scales, the science advancements and open questions in the interpretation of these results, current uncertainties as well fusion/cross-validation of GRACE/GRACE-FO data with other sensors and models.

sessions.name: Oceanography
sessions.description: This session invites presentations about advances in oceanographic applications of GRACE/GRACE-FO data products, including signal interpretation and model assimilation. Other topics include, but are not limited to, the validation of data products, the studies of regional or global oceanographic processes and sea level budgets, exploitation of GRACE/GRACE-FO data products jointly with data from other missions (such as GOCE), or other in situ oceanographic measurement systems (e.g. ARGO), etc.

sessions.name: Hydrology
sessions.description: Presentations reporting on advances in hydrological applications based on GRACE/GRACE-FO data products, including signal interpretation and model assimilation, the assessment of hydrological trends and long-term water storage variations, or GRACE/GRACE-FO data products that are optimized for terrestrial hydrology are invited to be submitted to this session

sessions.name: Multidisciplinary Science
sessions.description: This session is open for science topics which do not properly fit into the other available sessions. Also, if you are unsure about the right session for your abstract, please submit it to this session.

sessions.name: Towards the Operational Use of Satellite Gravimetry
sessions.description: This session focuses on the applications of GRACE/GRACE-FO, together with other remote sensing, in-situ, or numerical model data, to inform resource management, policy development, and decision-making at all time-scales. Some examples include EU's Copernicus Services, NASA's Applied Sciences Program, and other such efforts.

items.title: FEATS-G: Orbit and quantum sensor performance simulation for future satellite gravity missions
items.authors: Annike Knabe1, Henrik Wessel2, Stefanie Bremer2, and Matthias Weigelt1

affiliations.text: German Aerospace Center (DLR), Institute for Satellite Geodesy and Inertial Sensing, Hannover, Germany
German Aerospace Center (DLR), Institute for Satellite Geodesy and Inertial Sensing, Bremen, Germany

items.text: Satellite gravimetry missions GRACE and GRACE-FO have significantly advanced Earth observation by enabling monthly, high-precision mapping of global mass redistributions. These missions have provided unprecedented insights into the system Earth, such as ice sheet and glacier mass loss, sea level rise, terrestrial water storage changes. However, the classical electrostatic accelerometers suffer from their low-frequency drift and are one of the limiting factors. This drawback can be counterbalanced by an accelerometer based on Cold Atom Interferometry (CAI) because of its high long-term stability.The FEATS-G project advances this frontier through end-to-end simulations to evaluate quantum-based satellite mission concepts. The simulations allow for a comprehensive evaluation of future mission concepts and the exploration of novel scientific applications. They also enable the assessment of quantum-based sensors’ added value in distinguishing between different geophysical signals, while preparing the scientific community for the arrival of this new data type.This contribution focuses on the simulation procedure of observations based on quantum technology. The selected mission scenario will be simulated by the orbit propagation software VENQS. The satellites’ surface is modelled by means of finite elements in order to calculate precise non-gravitational forces induced by solar and Earth radiation and atmospheric drag. The non-gravitational accelerations are considered as disturbance and are measured by the accelerometer. The CAI acceleration measurements are simulated considering various error sources, such as detection noise, contrast loss, wavefront aberration and laser frequency noise. Furthermore, rotational effects and rotation compensation methods using a counter-rotating mirror are included. The simulation procedure and methodology and first results are shown. The artificial orbit data and sensor output will later be used in the gravity field recovery process.We acknowledge the support by the European Union for the project FEATS-G (Call: HORIZON-CL4-2025-02-SPACE-81).

items.title: Learning from ocean bottom pressure differences between GRACE and a state estimate constrained by GRACE
items.authors: Rui Ponte1, Nishchitha Silva1, Ou Wang2, Ichiro Fukumori2, and Mengnan Zhao1

affiliations.text: Atmospheric and Environmental Research, Lexington, MA, United States of America
Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, United States of America

items.text: Observations from GRACE and its follow-on mission have been used to constrain the ocean bottom pressure (OBP) fields in the state estimates produced by the project for Estimating the Circulation and Climate of the Ocean (ECCO). Here we examine the OBP residuals, i.e., the remaining differences between a recent optimized ECCO solution and the GRACE data, to identify potential issues with both the observations and the ocean model used in ECCO. The GRACE-ECCO residuals are dominated by long-term trends and seasonal variability and exhibit mostly large-scale structures. The trends can be partly related to unmodeled earthquake signals and gravitational, rotational and deformational (GRD) effects on the GRACE-derived OBP fields. Land hydrology processes and associated GRD effects can also contribute to seasonal residuals. In regions of high eddy energy (e.g., Agulhas Retroflection, Gulf Stream), residuals are partly caused by the impact of mesoscale signals on GRACE-derived OBP fields, which is not represented in the coarse-resolution ECCO model. Other possible contributions to the residuals include uncertainties in glacial isostatic adjustment models and poor horizontal resolution in both data (leakage of land signals in GRACE retrievals) and model (inadequate representation of coastal domains).

items.title: Towards hydrological extreme event monitoring using deep learning-downscaled simulated NGGM and MAGIC data and GRACE(-FO) observations
items.authors: Gilberto Goracci1, Celina Anael Farias2,3, and Ilias Daras4

affiliations.text: ESA Φ-lab Explore Office (EOP-S8E) - Climate Action, Sustainability and Science Dept. – Earth Observation Programmes Directorate

items.text:
Terrestrial Water Storage Anomalies (TWSA) derived from satellite gravimetry provide a unique, spatially integrated measure of large-scale hydrological conditions and are widely used to characterize basin-scale wet and dry states. However, their applicability to regional hydrological monitoring remains limited by their coarse spatial resolution, which hampers the detection of localized storage anomalies relevant to flood onset, evolution, and groundwater variability.
Here, it is investigated an unsupervised deep-learning framework based on convolutional neural networks to enhance the spatial resolution of TWSA products across simulated and real mission scenarios. The method relies on a U-Net architecture driven by ERA5-Land hydro-climatic variables, and is first applied to end-to-end closed-loop simulations of the NGGM and MAGIC next-generation gravity missions. Particular attention is given to 5-daily solutions, which represent a key expected advancement of future gravimetric constellations compared with the monthly solutions currently provided by GRACE(-FO). In this setting, simulated TWSA fields are downscaled from 3° to 1°, while monthly 2° simulations are also considered to assess the framework under GRACE-like temporal conditions. For the syntetic products, the downscaled fields are validated using the ESA Earth System Model 3.0 as the reference signal.
Results show that the downscaled products preserve consistency with native gravimetric observations while recovering finer-scale spatial structures. To assess transferability, the same pipeline is applied to real GRACE(-FO) observations, downscaling monthly 3° TWSA products into 1° maps.The framework is also extended to GRACE-derived groundwater storage anomalies (GWSA) over France, downscaled from 0.5° to 0.1° and evaluated against independent in situ groundwater observations.Finally, downscaled synthetic TWSA fields are exploited for extreme-event monitoring using threshold-based indicators derived from climatological anomalies. The analysis assesses whether the increased spatial resolution retains localized anomaly patterns otherwise smoothed at coarse scales, supporting the monitoring of flood-prone conditions.

items.title: Testing mascon regularization strategies for simulated future gravity-field recovery
items.authors: Josefine Wilms1, Christoph Dahle1, Markus Hauk1, Natalia Panafidina1, Michael Murboeck1,2, and Annette Eicker1

affiliations.text: Deutsches GeoForschungsZentrum GFZ, Section 1.2: Global Geomonitoring and Gravity Field, Weßling, Germany
Technische Universität Berlin, Fakultät VI Planen Bauen Umwelt, Institut für Geodäsie und Geoinformationstechnik, Berlin

items.text:
Mascon solutions estimate mass changes directly on predefined surface elements, rather than only representing them by spherical harmonic coefficients. They are useful for regional water storage, ice-mass, and ocean applications, and are already provided by several groups such as GSFC, JPL and CSR. In the framework of GRACE-C Science Data System preparations at GFZ, a project funded by DLR, we are developing and testing mascon processing strategies using realistic full-noise simulations of monthly gravity-field solutions.
We first consider a GRACE-C-like single polar-pair scenario, representing the continuation of the US-German GRACE mission series after GRACE and GRACE-FO. We then compare this with the proposed MAGIC double-pair constellation, an ESA-NASA concept in which the NASA/DLR GRACE-C polar pair is complemented by ESA’s inclined NGGM pair. By comparing the two scenarios, we investigate how the observation geometry affects the recovered mascon fields and the required regularization.
The processing starts from monthly spherical harmonic solutions. These are regularized in coefficient space before being transformed to the mascon grid. We test different spherical-harmonic regularization settings and inspect their effect on striping, ocean RMS, and land signal preservation.
In the mascon step, we compare two ways of building the regularization matrix. The first uses an intermediate mascon solution to construct a time-variable regularization matrix. The second derives the time-variable regularization matrix directly from synthesized spherical harmonic fields, avoiding the intermediate mascon step.
The recovered fields are compared with the known input signal to evaluate noise reduction and signal preservation. Preliminary results show that time-variable mascon regularization can reduce errors compared with the first mascon solution, but the best balance between noise reduction and signal preservation is still being evaluated. This work presents the current workflow, first results, and open questions for discussion.

items.title: Multiyear tropical warm pool warming drives slowdown in Antarctic mass loss
items.authors: Qinghua Ding, Yunhe Wang, Xiaofeng li, Thomas Ballinger, Yoshihiro Nakayama, Danial Topal, and Eric Steig

affiliations.text: University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, United States of America University of California Santa Barbara, Santa Barbara, United States of America

items.text: Antarctic mass loss has been a major contributor to global sea-level rise for most of the last few decades, mainly driven by West Antarctica1. During 2021–2023, however, a sharp increase in surface mass balance over Queen Mary Land and Wilkes Land in East Antarctica offset West Antarctic loss and slowed the rate of total ice mass loss2,3. Although this slowdown is consistent with the expected long-term precipitation response to global warming through poleward-shifted storm tracks and Antarctic moistening4, our results point to a different mechanism. Here we show that the recent ice mass gain was linked to a recurrent atmospheric teleconnection driven by sea surface temperature anomalies in the tropical warm pool, which experienced unusually persistent warming from 2021 to 2023 relative to the previous two decades. On the basis of observations and model experiments, we find that tropical warm pool warming excites a poleward-propagating Rossby-wave train that induces a high-pressure anomaly over East Antarctica, enhancing Queen Mary Land and Wilkes Land precipitation and driving the observed mass gain, with moisture primarily sourced from the mid-latitude Indian Ocean. Similar multiyear warming in the tropical warm pool recurs about once per decade in observations and historical simulations, and its influence on precipitation is distinct from the effects of global warming. Therefore, the recent Antarctic Ice Sheet mass gain is probably temporary and does not yet reflect a sustained, global-warming-driven moistening of Antarctica.

items.title: Antarctic and Greenland Ice Sheet Gravimetric Mass Balance from GRACE(-FO): TU Dresden’s ESA CCI+ Products and Component Partitioning for Antarctica
items.authors: Alexey Kupriyanov, Martin Horwath, Matthias O. Willen, and Thorben Döhne

affiliations.text: TUD Dresden University of Technology, Institute of Planetary Geodesy, Germany TUD Dresden University of Technology, Institute of Planetary Geodesy, Germany

items.text: For more than two decades, the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and its follow-on mission GRACE-FO have been providing unique information on mass changes occurring globally and in the Antarctic (AIS) and Greenland (GIS) ice sheets particularly. Ice sheets were assigned by the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS) as one of the essential climate variables. GRACE(-FO) observations showed that both AIS and GIS have an accelerating ice mass loss. Moreover, ice sheets are considered as one of the largest sources of uncertainty in future global sea-level rise projections. Therefore, consistent analysis of the ice sheet mass changes is needed for improving the understanding of their contribution to the global sea-level rise.We present the recently published extension (through December 2025) of the gravimetric mass balance (GMB) gridded and drainage basins products by TU Dresden for the AIS and GIS that was done in the framework of the European Space Agency's (ESA) Climate Change Initiative (CCI) projects. The products are based on the monthly GRACE(-FO) solutions CSR RL06.3 by the Center for Space Research at the University of Texas at Austin with applied tailored sensitivity kernel approach, developed at TU Dresden (Groh and Horwath 2021). For Antarctica a novelty of this release is a gap-filling interpolation for the 11-months GRACE/GRACE-FO transition period using the Regional Atmospheric Climate Model RACMO2.4p1. For the investigated period of more than 23 years, the GMB of the AIS was quantified to be −83±44 Gt a-1 and for GIS −246±14 Gt a-1, that corresponds to a mean sea-level rise of 0.23±0.12 mm a-1 and −0.68±0.04 mm a-1 respectively.The total mass change observed by GRACE(-FO) is the combined effect of variations in surface mass balance (SMB) changing ice-flow dynamics. The Partitioned GMB (GMBP) product is being developed to reflect these two physically distinct components. SMB variation effects are predominantly short-term or interannual and are controlled by ice-atmosphere interaction. Ice-flow dynamics effects, in contrast, are mostly long-term (decadal or longer), controlled by ice-ocean interaction and most crucial for understanding long-term evolution of the ice sheet. We present preliminary methods and results of the Partitioned GMB.

items.title: GRACE and satellite altimetry to measure ocean mass and density changes between 2002 and 2026
items.authors: Ernst Schrama and Wouter van der Wal

affiliations.text: TU Delft, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Space Department, Delft, Netherlands TU Delft, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Space Department, Delft, Netherlands

items.text: From GRACE and GRACE-FO we get time variable information from the Earth’s gravity field since 2002. The monthly time series obtained from science centers can be represented as a surface water layer. By sampling the oceans at mascons we obtain a mass against time signal which represents the barystatic component of the sea level rise signal which is confronted with satellite altimetry since 1992, the combination of both geodetic results allows to estimate the density change in the ocean domain for which profiling float measurements can be used as an independent source. Of particular interest is the effect of glacial isostatic adjustment which shows up in both gravimetry and altimetry. The GIA correction determines for a part the implementation of the geocenter correction that is used during the GRACE data processing. Depending on the processing choices to represent ocean mass and the GIA correction that is required we find barystatic sea level rates varying between 1.9 and 2.4 mm/yr whereby we remark that the uncertainty is larger than previously expected. The volume change in the oceans is remarkably stable, it remains at 3.7 mm/yr with a noticeable acceleration of 0.2 mm/yr2. This means that the density change due to temperature and salinity changes in the ocean domain varies between 1.3 and 1.8 mm/yr.

items.title: Uncovering the Onset of Water Storage Droughts in the Danube River Basin
items.authors: Eva Boergens1, Sangita Chouhan1, and Julian Haas2

affiliations.text: GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, Sec. 1.3 Earth System Modelling, Potsdam, Germany
GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences, Sec. 4.4 Hydrology, Potsdam, Germany

items.text: Over the past decade, Europe has experienced several interconnected droughts. Since 2018, TWS has shown no storage surplus across the majority of Central Europe. However, does this truly mark the onset of these drought conditions, or did they start earlier? To answer this question, we apply the BFAST (Breaks For Additive Season and Trend) method to detect breakpoints in the TWS time series, aiming to pinpoint the onset of the ongoing drought. Here, we focus on the Danube River Basin. Since TWS represents the sum of all water storage compartments (WSCs) — groundwater storage, surface water storage, root-zone soil moisture, snow water equivalent, and glacier storage — we further investigate datasets for each individual WSC. Since hydro-meteorological fluxes, namely precipitation and evapotranspiration, are the significant drivers of TWS changes, we also include relevant hydro-meteorological indices (SPI, SPEI, EDDI) in the study.BFAST identifies a significant breakpoint in TWS as early as 2015, and an even earlier one in groundwater storage in 2013, while soil moisture remains stable throughout. Investigation of the hydro-meteorological drivers of storage change reveals that precipitation remained stable over the full study period (2002-2025), and that the observed decline in water storage is instead attributable to increased evapotranspiration driven by rising temperatures.Further analysis confirms the significance of the 2015 breakpoint in TWS: storage was stable beforehand but has declined significantly since. The temporal behaviour of storage is examined further using a transition matrix and a duration frequency analysis. Prior to 2015, TWS remained predominantly in a normal state, whereas after 2015 it exhibited more frequent and prolonged dry periods. These results confirm the significance of the ongoing shift in the hydrological system of the Danube River Basin in recent years.

items.text:
Accurate and continuous determination of the Earth’s time-variable gravity field is essential for monitoring mass redistribution related to hydrological, climatic, and geodynamic processes. GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) have demonstrated the high capability of low-low satellite-to-satellite tracking (LL-SST) technique for global gravity field recovery; however, the resulting accuracy strongly depends on the quality of the involved sensors, e.g., the accelerometers (ACC) used to account for non-gravitational forces. While conventional electrostatic accelerometers (EA) provide high short-term sensitivity, their performance is affected by drift at low frequencies. Emerging quantum-based sensors, particularly Cold Atom Interferometry (CAI) accelerometers, offer promising characteristics to overcome the later issue for future satellite gravimetry.
This study investigates accelerometer observation transplantation to reduce the number of accelerometers required onboard future satellite gravimetry missions. Different configurations involving EA, CAI, and hybrid EA–CAI accelerometers are evaluated using closed-loop LL-SST simulations. Four scenarios are considered, ranging from the conventional EA-only configuration to an ideal configuration in which both satellites carry complete hybrid accelerometers. Particular attention is given to a reduced-sensor configuration in which EA and CAI observations are transplanted between satellites, enabling a virtual hybrid configuration with fewer physical accelerometers.
In addition to conventional analytical transplantation, machine-learning (ML) approaches, including Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM), are investigated to improve the transplanted accelerometer observations. The configurations are evaluated directly at the gravity-field level. The results show that the complete dual-hybrid configuration provides the highest performance, while the ML-based reduced-sensor configuration significantly improves upon analytical transplantation and approaches the performance of the ideal hybrid configuration.
The data-driven transplantation concept is further assessed using real GRACE accelerometer observations. During GRACE and GRACE-FO, accelerometer degradation or failure affected the availability and quality of non-gravitational acceleration observations, requiring their reconstruction. An LSTM-based dynamic mapping using GRACE-A accelerometer observations and auxiliary non-gravitational force models is developed to reconstruct GRACE-B accelerations. The reconstructed observations are introduced into monthly gravity field recovery and evaluated through degree variances, equivalent-water-height representations, and RMS variability over the oceans. The results demonstrate successful reconstruction of the missing accelerometer information and improvements in the resulting monthly gravity field solutions. The same framework can also be adapted to degraded accelerometer observations in GRACE-FO.
Overall, the results demonstrate the potential of ML for recovering missing or degraded accelerometer observations and enabling reduced-sensor architectures for future satellite gravimetry. Combining quantum sensing, accelerometer transplantation, and ML provides a promising pathway toward high-performance, less complex, and potentially more cost-effective future gravimetry missions.
Keywords: Satellite gravimetry; GRACE; GRACE-FO; accelerometer transplantation; Cold Atom Interferometry; hybrid accelerometers; machine learning; time-variable gravity field.

items.title: When and where does groundwater recharge occur in arid lands?
items.authors: Mohamed Sultan, Hassan Saleh, and Rami W Mansouri

affiliations.text: Western Michigan University, Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, KALAMAZOO, United States of America Western Michigan University, Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences, KALAMAZOO, United States of America

items.text: Isotopic and geochronologic evidence indicates that many aquifers in arid lands were recharged during past wetter climatic periods, yet where and when modern recharge occurs remains poorly constrained. By integrating GRACE and GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage (TWS) observations, GPM precipitation data, groundwater-level measurements, and groundwater isotopic compositions, we documented aquifer recharge following tropical cyclones and extreme precipitation events in Oman’s karstic aquifers and the fractured-basalt aquifers of western Arabia. We then extended the analysis across nine geographic domains defined by continental location and the boundaries of the major arid zones. Our results show that extreme precipitation events generated groundwater storage responses detectable by GRACE across approximately two-thirds of arid regions, with recharge efficiencies exceeding conventional estimates based on long-term averages of precipitation and recharge. These findings indicate that GRACE TWS records carry more information about episodic groundwater recharge than previously recognized. The forthcoming GRACE-C mission will help minimize gaps in the monthly TWS record, and the Next Generation Gravity Mission (NGGM) will provide enhanced spatial and temporal resolution for refining estimates of modern aquifer recharge.

items.title: Impact of Heterogeneous Mantle Viscosity on the Glacial Isostatic Adjustment Correction for GRACE(‐FO): Implications for Surface Mass Trends
items.authors: Erin Hightower1, Lambert Caron1, Felix Landerer1, Michael Watkins2,3, Erik Ivins1, and Eric Larour1

affiliations.text: Solid Earth and Ice Group, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA USA

items.text: Accurate interpretation of time‐variable gravity from GRACE(‐FO) requires correction for glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), which has a gravitational signal similar in magnitude to that of contemporary hydrological and cryospheric mass change. Traditional GIA models used to correct space gravimetry data assume a radially symmetric mantle viscosity structure, ignoring the 3D structure evident in seismic tomography. We quantify the sensitivity of GRACE‐derived surface mass trends to laterally heterogeneous mantle viscosity by computing a suite of global GIA models using the finite‐element code CitcomSVE. We utilize 3D viscosity fields derived from tomography and two commonly used ice‐loading histories, systematically increasing heterogeneity about their associated radial viscosity profiles. GIA solutions are converted to GRACE‐compatible Stokes coefficients and equivalent water height to recompute GRACE mass trends. While global mean ocean and Greenland ice mass trends are weakly affected, regional terrestrial water storage and ocean mass patterns exhibit large and spatially coherent changes. 3D GIA corrections lead to significantly more drying conditions in Canada and slightly more drying conditions throughout most land‐masses, can lead to a reduction in the long‐term rate of ice mass loss in Antarctica, and can reverse the ocean mass trend in key ocean basins. Models combining elevated lower‐mantle viscosity with strong lateral heterogeneity eliminate problematic GRACE ocean anomalies in the eastern North Atlantic and potentially resolve the disagreement between GIA‐ and geodynamics‐derived estimates of mantle viscosity. Our results demonstrate that realistic 3D viscosity is essential for quantifying and reducing GIA‐related uncertainty in GRACE interpretations and can ultimately lead to improved confidence in the inferred surface mass changes.

items.authors: Marius Schlaak1, Julia Pfeffer2, Roland Pail3, Marie Bouih2, Alejandro Blazquez1, Benoit Meyssignac1, and Ilias Daras4

items.text: The ESA-SING dataset has been created within the ESA-SING project to investigate current and future satellite gravity mission concepts. These synthetic observations support mission-impact studies within the ESA-SING project, evaluating the added value of the NGGM and MAGIC missions for scientific applications and operational services in hydrology, ocean sciences, glaciology, climate sciences, solid earth sciences, and geodesy.The ESA-SING synthetic observations are based on input models representing global mass changes over a 12-year period available from the ESA Earth System Model, incorporating realistic instrument errors and background uncertainties for tidal and non-tidal de-aliasing products. The uncertainties in simulated single polar pair missions are comparable to those in historical GRACE records, as confirmed by the consistency in barystatic sea level errors between GRACE and GRACE-C-like data.The ESA-SING dataset contains a 12-year time series of 30-day and 5-day estimates of the time-variable gravity field, together with estimates of the long-term trend and annual cycle, representing the ESM-simulated mass transport in the hydrosphere, cryosphere and Solid Earth and incorporating realistic uncertainties for each mission configuration. Simulated satellite gravimetry products are available in spherical harmonics (L2) and equivalent water height (L3) grids for three mission concepts: a single inline-pair in polar orbit (GRACE-C-like), a single pair in an inclined orbit (NGGM), and the combination of both (MAGIC). By evaluating the recoverability of time-variable mass signals across multiple temporal scales, The ESA-SING dataset yields representative error estimates for all three satellite constellations.This work provides an overview of the SING simulations and assesses the performance of the satellite configurations considered, demonstrating that the future inclined pair (NGGM) and double-pair (MAGIC) concepts reduce noise levels in time-variable gravity field retrievals compared to single-pair observations. Moreover, this contribution will provide an introduction to the ESA-SING dataset to assist potential users.

items.title: Ocean mass changes from the lower degree harmonics of the GRACE/GFO monthly gravity fields.
items.authors: Per Knudsen and Ole Andersen

affiliations.text: DTU Space, National Space Institute, Geodesy, Kgs. Lyngby, Denmark DTU Space, National Space Institute, Geodesy, Kgs. Lyngby, Denmark

items.text: The study is based on the low degree harmonics to focus on the accurate long wavelength parts of the GRACE/GFO gravity fields. To reduce the contamination of mass changes on land a set of point masses are estimated and analyzed to verify estimates of the melting of the major ice sheets. Subsequently, residual gravity fields are used to recover characteristics and regional patterns of changes in the ocean mass.Initially, ocean mass changes are computed using the direct approach using coefficients filtered at harmonic degree and order 20, 40 and 60. The results show that smoothed GSM fields may be used as well, though a wider buffer zone is required. In all cases, values for the global mean ocean mass trends of 2.13-2.47 mm/y were found which are pretty consistent with what others had found already.The second part focus on using the lower degree and more accurate parts of the GRACE/GFO gravity fields. A method for removing land signals contaminating the ocean signal, is tested. It is based on point masses. Though the locations of the point masses at fixed grid nodes may not be optimal, the method seems to work well. The total mass loss on land is about 660 Gt corresponding to 1.83 mm/y ocean sea level gain which is on the low side compared to the values from the initial study. However, using the residual fields from where the continental signals have been removed and no buffer zone, a trend of 1.82 mm/y is obtained. Hence, there is a very good agreement with the corresponding land value. The results show that the method is very successful in removing land signal from the GRACE/GFO monthly fields and facilitates further studies of the changes in the ocean masses.

items.title: From tight to wide deadband: where current model-based GRACE-FO transplants fall behind
items.authors: Frederik Jacobs, Miguel Cuadrat-Grzybowski, and Christian Siemes

affiliations.text: TU Delft, Aerospace Engineering, Astrodynamics and Space Missions, Delft, Netherlands TU Delft, Aerospace Engineering, Astrodynamics and Space Missions, Delft, Netherlands

items.text: One of the GRACE-FO satellites has a malfunctioning accelerometer, rendering it largely unusable for gravity field retrieval. To mitigate the impact, replacement accelerations have been made available, the so-called accelerometer transplants. Several transplants have been developed by different institutes, following either a data-driven approach (the JPL transplant), which assumes that the non-gravitational acceleration is common to both spacecraft and may include empirical corrections, or a model-driven approach (the TU Graz and ZARM transplants), which assumes common atmospheric conditions. Last year, we presented a model-driven transplant developed at TU Delft for the GRACE mission, informed by high-fidelity aerodynamic and radiation-pressure modeling. In this work, we extend that transplant to GRACE-FO.Previous work on GRACE could assess transplant quality by comparing the transplanted acceleration with the measured acceleration for the period when both accelerometers were still operating. In contrast, GRACE-FO offers this opportunity only for a few weeks after launch, when the aerodynamic acceleration is very small, so quality is instead assessed through gravity field retrieval. All transplants, including the JPL, TU Graz and ZARM products, are processed through a single, identical gravity field retrieval using the GROOPS software, so that any differences between solutions can be attributed to the transplant itself. We evaluate the solutions using the open-ocean RMS of equivalent water height, degree-amplitude spectra, and spatial maps after removing bias and trend from a reference field.To mitigate small fuel leaks, the GRACE-FO satellites changed attitude mode in 2023. Before 2023, the satellites were in tight-deadband mode, requiring many thruster firings but keeping a stable attitude. Since 2023, they have been in wide-deadband mode, needing fewer firings but allowing larger attitude variations. We compare transplant quality across both modes using six months distributed across the mission, selected to separate the effect of the attitude mode from that of solar activity and sun-orbit geometry.In tight-deadband mode, the TU Delft model-driven transplant is competitive with the operational data-driven JPL product. In wide-deadband mode, we observe increased noise in the gravity field models from the TU Delft transplant compared to those obtained with the JPL transplant. We attribute this observation to the amplification of modeling errors from different sources, such as gas-surface interaction models, atmospheric models, and attitude errors, to which model-based transplants are inherently sensitive.

items.title: Advancing glacier and ice-sheet mass-change observations with GRACE-C, NGGM and MAGIC
items.authors: Ingo Sasgen1 and Bert Wouters2

affiliations.text: Alfred-Wegener-Institute Bremerhaven, Geosciences Department / Section Glaciology, Bremerhaven, Germany
Department of Geoscience and Remote Sensing, Delft University of Technology, Delft, The Netherlands

items.text: GRACE and GRACE-FO have transformed observations of glacier and ice-sheet mass change, but their monthly solutions and correlated noise limit the detection of short-lived melt and accumulation events, and long-term ice-dynamic signals. We assess ESA’s inclined Next Generation Gravity Mission (NGGM; ~70° inclination), which provides denser, more uniform sampling throughout the non-polar latitude band than a near-polar pair. End-to-end simulations with ESA-funded SING project show that NGGM improves the recovery of lower-latitude glacier mass change, more clearly resolving seasonal variability and long-term trends, showing additional potential for hydrological applications. For Greenland and Antarctica, NGGM improves sensitivity to short-lived melt and accumulation events and provides independent constraints on long-term accelerations in ice-dynamic discharge. Within MAGIC, NGGM complements the near-polar GRACE-C pair to provide more homogeneous near-global observations of glaciers and ice sheets, strengthening constraints on regional climate and ice-sheet models and future sea-level rise.

items.title: Arctic glacier mass change from GRACE/GRACE-FO: Regional variability, atmospheric drivers and rapid GIA
items.authors: Ingo Sasgen

affiliations.text: Alfred-Wegener-Institute Bremerhaven, Geosciences Department / Section Glaciology, Bremerhaven, Germany Alfred-Wegener-Institute Bremerhaven, Geosciences Department / Section Glaciology, Bremerhaven, Germany

items.text: Arctic glaciers are losing mass rapidly, but their regional variability reflects both atmospheric forcing and solid-Earth processes. We combine GRACE/GRACE-FO glacier mass balances with ESA CCI Permafrost and CALM observations to investigate common drivers of glacier melt and permafrost thaw. Two dominant modes of summer atmospheric circulation explain about 75% of their common pan-Arctic variability over 2002–2022. We further show that rapid viscoelastic rebound in low-viscosity regions such as Alaska and Iceland can substantially bias gravimetry-derived glacier trends if not accounted for. Together with recent GlaMBIE assessments, these results provide a broader view of Arctic glacier change, its climatic drivers, and remaining observational uncertainties.

items.authors: Judith Garnier1, Alejandro Blazquez3, Alexandre Boughanemi1, Fabien Gachet4, Emeric Lavergne2, Julien Lefebve3, Jean-Michel Lemoine4, Delphine Leroux2, Eric Pellereau1, and Julia Pfeffer1

items.text: GRACE and GRACE-FO satellite missions measure the spatial and temporal variations in the Earth’s gravity field at a spatial resolution of around 300 kilometers. Unlike most gravity field products available at monthly resolutions, the CNES produces a 10-day Level 2 solution constrained by Satellite Laser Ranging using Singular Value Decomposition and Tikhonov regularization, improving the estimation of the low- and high-degree spherical harmonics. Resolved up to degree 90 without spatial filtering, this product enhances the spatial resolution of satellite gravity products. Here, we present the hydrological applications of the Level 3 product, corrected for the missing degree 1 and Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA), representing Terrestrial Water Storage Anomalies (TWSA) expressed in gridded Equivalent Water Heights (mmEWH).This study assesses the added value of the 10-day CNES product for monitoring extreme hydrological events such as droughts and floods based on GRACE-Drought Severity Index (GRACE-DSI). Results show that the 10-day product captures major events like the 2010-2011 La Niña in Australia, and the severe drought that affected France during the 2022 summer. Comparison with the monthly CNES ensemble and daily ITSG-2018 products confirms the strong temporal consistency at seasonal to interannual time scales and substantially higher spatial and temporal resolutions of the CNES 10-day product.GRACE-DSI also shows good agreement with in situ indicators, particularly those integrating information over long time scales, such as the Palmer Drought Severity Index and the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). By accounting for the total terrestrial water storage variability, integrated from the surface to deep aquifers, the GRACE-DSI complements indices targeting individual components of the hydrological cycle. The improved temporal and spatial resolution makes the 10-day CNES product and the associated 10-day GRACE-DSI particularly relevant for the monitoring of extreme hydrological events. This study also suggests potential for the preparation of hydrological applications of the future satellite gravimetry missions NGGM and MAGIC, with expected higher spatio-temporal resolution and shorter latency time.

items.text: Since 2002, the GRACE and GRACE-FO satellite missions have been monitoring monthly variations in the gravitational field caused by mass redistributions within the Earth’s system. To extract information on the global and regional water cycle, estimates of the gravity field must be corrected to account for several instrumental and geophysical processes. The SAGSA L3 dataset uses an ensemble approach to estimate water mass redistributions in the ocean, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and cryosphere, as well as their uncertainties. Here, we review the processing and post-processing steps included in the ensemble approach, with a particular focus on the dry mass of the atmosphere and leakage from the continents to the oceans. A small-amplitude drift has been identified in the global average estimate of atmospheric mass, affecting the standard ERA-5 reanalysis and all dealiasing models derived from it. We show that the global atmospheric mass correction has a significant impact on ocean applications, reducing the sea level budget residuals by approximately 2 mm between 2016 and 2026. items.text: GOCO2025s is a global gravity field model represented by spherical harmonic coefficients up to degree and order 300, with constrained secular, annual, and semi-annual variations up to degree and order 200. It is derived from 23 years of satellite data, incorporating observations from the dedicated gravity field missions Gravity field and steady-state Ocean Circulation Explorer (GOCE), Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE), and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO), as well as kinematic orbits of 18 low Earth orbit satellites and satellite laser ranging observations to 9 passive geodetic satellites. The complementary measurement principles of the different satellite missions and their strengths in determining specific parts of the spherical harmonic spectrum were exploited by combining the data at the normal equation level, with emphasis on the stochastic modeling of each contribution. Particular focus was placed on the inclusion of GRACE-FO laser ranging interferometer (LRI) data, which provided the dominant contribution to the estimation of the spherical harmonic coefficients between degrees 70 and 200. All processing steps, except for the determination of the GOCE normal equations, were carried out at the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology (TUG) employing up-to-date background models. The consistent in-house processing of nearly all satellite data, using the Gravity Recovery Object Oriented Programming System (GROOPS) software package, minimized errors arising from inconsistencies of different algorithms or models being applied.The individual files of the GOCO2025s model (Öhlinger et al., 2025) are available at the TUG repository and identified with the following DOI: 10.3217/f48p8-8h651. They comprise the static and time-dependent gravity field coefficients and their respective uncertainty information, all parts of the normal equation system of the static gravity field, and the gravitational potential of non-tidal atmospheric and ocean masses already included in GOCO2025s.

items.text: GFZ aims to distribute a reprocessed and improved RL07 Level-2 gravity field time series in the last quarter of 2026. Most of these improvements have been developed within the Research Unit “New Refined Observations of Climate Change from Spaceborne Gravity Missions” (NEROGRAV) funded by the German Research Foundation DFG.When developing the new GFZ RL07 processing standards, the main focus was on an optimized stochastic modeling during the GRACE/GRACE-FO gravity field determination. This includes the extension of the stochastic instrument error models, the optimization of the combination of the different observations in terms of relative weighting, and the inclusion of non-tidal background model error variance-covariance information in the adjustment process. Further changes compared to GFZ RL06 comprise the parameterization as well as the applied background models, e.g., the ocean tide model and the static gravity field model.This presentation provides an overview of the GFZ RL07 performance compared to RL06 with focus at specific processing aspects and its impact on the gravity field solution, such as the ocean tide model update or the influence of stochastic modelling of observation and background model errors. Improvements stemming from the applied advanced processing strategy led to a significant reduction of noise (> 30% relative to GFZ RL06), as well as more realistic formal uncertainties of the estimated gravity field parameters. In addition, a short outlook on the expected performance of LRI-based GRACE-FO gravity field performance is presented.

items.text: Total Drainable Water Storage (TDWS) represents the portion of basin water storage that can drain and sustain river discharge, providing a basin-scale indicator of freshwater availability. Reliable global estimation of TDWS could therefore improve assessments of freshwater availability and help identify basins with limited capacity to sustain discharge. However, estimating TDWS globally from space-based Terrestrial Water Storage Anomalies (TWSA) remains constrained by both satellite-observation errors and differences in basin hydrological behavior. We use closed-loop satellite gravimetry simulations incorporating realistic instrumental and aliasing errors to estimate TDWS for mission configurations representative of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Continuity (GRACE-C), the Next Generation Gravity Mission (NGGM), and the Mass-change and Geosciences International Constellation (MAGIC). Assuming a linear runoff–storage (R–S) relationship, TDWS is estimated for more than 200 globally distributed river basins. Two independent Earth system model realizations, ESA ESM2.0 and ESM3.0, are used as reference TWSA datasets. Mission-based TDWS estimates are evaluated against their corresponding references, and retrieval errors are examined in relation to basin area, directional shape, storage and discharge variability, terrain relief, land cover, climate, and R–S linearity. NGGM and MAGIC consistently improve TDWS estimation relative to GRACE-C. Median relative errors decrease from 7.9% for GRACE-C to 4.2% and 4.3% for NGGM and MAGIC, respectively, under ESM2.0, and to 4.5% and 4.1% under ESM3.0. The largest size-dependent improvements occur for basins between 200,000 and 500,000 km², with error reductions of about five percentage points relative to GRACE-C. Directional basin geometry also affects retrieval performance, with improvements increasing toward strongly north–south-oriented basins under ESM3.0. Environmental controls remain evident: rugged basins generally show larger TDWS errors than flat basins, while under ESM3.0 MAGIC reduces the median error in polar climates from 10.0% to 4.4%. The reference R–S relationship achieves a Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of at least 0.7 in 86% of basins under ESM2.0 and 79% under ESM3.0. NGGM and MAGIC reproduce the reference NSE more closely than GRACE-C, demonstrating the benefit of improved gravity-field recovery. Nevertheless, improved satellite observations cannot compensate for a weak or unsuitable R–S relationship. These simulations therefore provide more than a comparison of future mission performance: they identify the observational, geometric, and hydrological conditions that control basin-scale TDWS retrieval. Moving toward robust global TDWS estimation will require both next-generation satellite gravimetry and basin-specific assessments of hydrological retrieval suitability.

items.text: So far, the operational combination of the monthly GRACE, or GRACE-FO gravity field solutions by the Combination Service of Time-variable Gravity fields (COST-G) has been performed on the solution level. The originally foreseen combination on the normal equation (NEQ) level suffered from the very diverse and not realistic formal uncertainties, which hampered the application of Variance Component Estimation (VCE) and made the use of empirical weighting factors mandatory. Meanwhile, empirical noise models that enable the determination of realistic formal uncertainties are available from several GRACE-FO analysis centers. Experimental NEQ-combinations confirmed the applicability of VCE for the GRACE-FO combination and also the combination with SLR turned out to be feasible without the use of empirical weighting factors. The combination of the future GRACE-C and NGGM missions on the NEQ-level is a prerequisite to generate gravity field solutions of the MAGIC constellation. Consequently, the combination of NEQs from different Analysis Centers (ACs), including also SLR, will be the goal of future COST-G releases, but relies on the cooperation of the ACs to provide their NEQs and to apply realistic noise models.

items.text: This study processes over a decade of space geodetic observations from Low Earth Orbiters (LEO; e.g., GRACE, Jason, and Sentinel series), dedicated Satellite Laser Ranging platforms (SLR; e.g., LAGEOS-1/2, LARES), and GPS ground and satellite tracking networks to simultaneously realize the terrestrial reference frame and recover low-degree time-variable gravity coefficients at the observation level. Building upon this unified multi-technique processing framework, we expand our processing strategy to incorporate GRACE-FO onboard accelerometer data and inter-satellite ranging data. By leveraging the dynamic connection between frame realization and gravity estimation inside a single, consistent processing framework, our approach directly resolves low-degree spherical harmonic terms, including geocenter motion (degree-1), J2, and J3. Finally, we evaluate the consistency of these observation-level low-degree gravity solutions against established products, specifically Technical Notes 13 and 14 as well as independent SLR-derived estimates, demonstrating the capability of this integrated framework to provide a robust, independent alternative for low degree gravity field determination.© 2026. items.text: The DANSk-LSM (Developing Efficient Multi-Sensor Data Assimilation Frameworks for Integrating Earth Observation Satellite Data into Land Surface Models) project, funded by Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), developed and demonstrated physically consistent and computationally efficient data assimilation frameworks for hydrological modelling. Between 2022 and 2026, the project integrated multi-source Earth observation data into land surface models to improve monitoring and forecasting of hydrological extremes.A major outcome was the assimilation of GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage (TWS) observations together with satellite-derived surface soil moisture and recently the addition of surface water dynamics is being explored. Novel data assimilation settings were developed and evaluated across diverse river basins (e.g., Brahmaputra, Danube and Mississippi), improving the representation of water storage variations, fluxes, and drought and flood evolution. Scientific and implementation challenges were also identified.DANSk-LSM delivered open-access tools, including PyGLDA software, and high-resolution signle sensor and multi-sensor data assimilation tools. The project also fostered collaboration across geodesy, remote sensing, hydrology, and data science communities, laying the groundwork for next-generation Digital Twin Earth hydrology systems and future satellite gravity missions. items.title: GRACE Data as Non-Tidal Deformation in Reference Frame Determination: From Position Timeseries Forecast to Frame Realization

affiliations.text: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology

items.text: The terrestrial reference frame (TRF) is the foundation for all space-based, airborne, and ground-based Earth observations. The accuracy of position data ultimately depends on the accuracy of TRF, which consists of precise Earth-centered coordinates of hundred of surface sites, many of which anchor the orbit estimates of the global navigation satellites.The non-tidal deformation (NTD) due to loading from atmosphere, ocean, and ground water tends to seasonally modulate the space geodetic position data used in determination of TRF. Campaign to determine the International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF) takes place approximately every 5 years (with a recent initiative to realize intra-campaign ITRF updates every year). Because of such latency in ITRF realizations, forecasts of the TRF positions are desired in a typical application, relying on the TRF velocity estimate to forecast the linear trajectory projection. Here, we examine how various models of NTD could affect the accuracy of such TRF position trajectory forecasts.In particular, we have seen that GRACE-based surface deformation data can be used as proxy of NTD in estimation of the site velocity. At individual GNSS sites, use of the GRACE data were particularly effective in mitigating extremely large forecast errors at certain sites, out-performing the standard ITRF NTD estimation method (via a fit to a truncated Fourier series) by an average of 3 mm. Also, no degradation of the forecasts due to addition of the GRACE data was observed. In order to extend the use of the GRACE-based deformation data to a TRF realization, we need to address: (1) the temporal coverage of the GRACE data, such as the gap between GRACE and GRACE-FO and pre-2003 period; (2) compatibility in site-to-site spatial correlations exhibited by GRACE versus TRF site position data. We show that the spatio-temporal behavior of the GRACE deformation data can be "learned" empirically via multichannel singular spectrum analysis (MSSA) to fill the GRACE/GRACE-FO gap. The MSSA GRACE data have improved the forecast accuracy in the gap where we have resorted to linear interpolation in the past, and the improved forecasts in the gap period were statistically indistinguishable from the period with actual GRACE data. This encourages consideration for hindcasting the GRACE data into a much longer 1997-2003 period for the use in a full TRF realization.

items.text: Satellite altimetry missions have transformed our capability to observe ice sheet surface elevation change with unprecedented spatial precision. While altimetry excels at localized surface height changes, converting height to mass requires firn air content corrections. Conversely, satellite gravimetry (GRACE/GRACE-FO) directly measures mass change with high accuracy over large scales, but is limited to coarse spatial resolutions (~300 km).Here, we present a formal data combination framework integrating two decades (2002–2020) of satellite altimetry observations (ICESat, ICESat-2, CryoSat-2, Envisat, ERS-2) with GRACE/GRACE-FO Level-1 data at the level of the gravimetry normal equations. By solving for 1 degree circular disk mascon elements, altimetry observations dominate the inversion at individual mascon scales, breaking inter-mascon spatial correlations and localizing signals over dynamic glacier catchments like Pine Island, Thwaites, and Totten Glaciers. Gravimetry dominates at long spatial wavelengths, preserving continental and basin-scale mass balance accuracy.The monthly Antarctic mass change solution achieves an effective spatial resolution of (100 km)2 , fulfilling long-standing community target requirements. Applying mass-conserving gain factors derived from altimetry spatial fields further yields downscaled monthly mass change at a 1.92 km scale. items.text: The overall error in gravity field products derived from satellite-to-satellite tracking gravity missions like the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (GRACE-FO) is driven by a combination of temporal aliasing error, and measurement system error consisting of both stochastic and deterministic sources. While the impact of each of these error sources has been extensively documented in the literature, there has been relatively little study of how the phasing of deterministic errors, or tones, propagates into the gravity field solution. Because these errors are primarily driven by on-orbit thermal variations, this study uses flight data from GRACE-FO thermistors alongside high-fidelity thermo-mechanical simulations that map temperature variations to structural deformation to investigate the phase and amplitude of these tones.We utilize these data to derive the most probable phasing of twice-per-revolution tones in both inter-satellite ranging and accelerometer measurements. We are particularly interested in the interplay of these tones and the twice-per-revolution component of absolute frequency error in the inter-satellite ranging signal. Unlike once-per-revolution errors, which are largely filtered out by empirical parameterization during standard orbit determination, twice-per-revolution errors survive the filtering process and map directly into the estimated gravity field. While we exclusively use GRACE-FO data and numerical simulations of the GRACE-Continuity flight system in this work, the principles of this work apply to any gravity mission using an inter-satellite ranging system. We demonstrate that tone phasing plays a critical role in the magnitude of the resulting gravity field degree variance, particularly in C20. We conclude by discussing strategies to account for deterministic measurement system errors.

items.title: Ellipsoidal Equal-Area Panel Mascons from GRACE Intersatellite Geopotential Differences: A Preliminary Assessment over China
items.authors: Vagner Ferreira1, Yongzhao Fan1, Thomas Grombein2, Kurt Seitz2, and Hansjörg Kutterer2

affiliations.text: Hohai University, School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Nanjing, China

items.text: We present a mascon-type solution that partitions the Earth's surface into contiguous, gap-free, equal-area panels defined directly on the reference ellipsoid via an authalic-latitude mapping, eliminating the need for a constant-radius approximation or subsequent rescaling. Each panel is treated as a locally curved point mass, yielding a closed-form kernel for the GRACE intersatellite geopotential differences (GPD), which serve as observations. Panel masses are estimated in a Bayesian (maximum a posteriori) framework using a diagonal prior covariance informed by the temporal variability of an independent hydrological field. The regularized normal equations are solved by preconditioned conjugate-gradient least squares (CGLS) with L-curve stopping, avoiding the assembly or factorization of any large matrix and enabling the full monthly inversion to run on standard workstation hardware. Based on this framework, a preliminary global inversion was performed for 4,704 ellipsoidal panels for each of 155 monthly WHU/SGG GPD datasets spanning April 2002 to July 2016. For a preliminary assessment, the results were clipped to China and evaluated against the official JPL, CSR, and GSFC mascon solutions. Overall, the solution reproduces the dominant spatial patterns, seasonal amplitude, and secular trends of the reference products, with spatial correlations ranging from 0.73 to 0.82 for annual amplitude and 0.67 to 0.74 for trend, and a spatial correlation of 0.80 with JPL-M for a single-month (September 2005) verification. Basin-averaged time series for China's nine major river basins reproduce reported drought events, with discrepancies against the reference mascons confined mainly to an arid basin. These results demonstrate that the proposed ellipsoidal-panel parametrization offers an efficient, transparent, and reproducible alternative for regional mass inversion.

items.text:
This study directly utilises GRACE Level-1B (L1B) KBR post-fit residuals, provided by the Center for Space Research, as the basis for high-frequency mass change modelling. We showcase the updated methodology and its uncertainty characteristics, demonstrating the potential of KBR post-fit residuals to recover sub-monthly surface mass variations from the GRACE(-FO) mission by exploiting information already contained in the conventional monthly gravity-field processing chain, without requiring additional observations or a separate high-frequency gravity-field inversion. We submitted the work to the Journal of Geodesy, and it continues the methodology presented in our previous Science Meeting contribution. 

The methodology combines geo-fits with post-fit residuals from the KBR instrument of the GRACE satellites. Geo-fits represent the range-rate L1B observations fitted to monthly spherical harmonic gravity models in traditional least-squares gravity retrieval. The post-fit residuals represent the instantaneous discrepancies between the reduced observations (pre-fits) and the corresponding geo-fits, and therefore contain information not represented by the monthly gravity-field solution. We spatially interpolate 5-day sets of post-fit residuals and combine them with the corresponding spatially binned monthly geo-fits, resulting in gridded high-frequency (HF) geo-fits. We then transform the HF geo-fits into equivalent water height (EWH) using an empirical relationship. 

Since the previous study, the methodology has been further developed in several aspects. The updated framework considers residuals in both the range and line-of-sight gravity difference (LGD) domains, providing three formulations: Range, LGD, and a hybrid formulation. The latter uses a weighted and normalised combination of both observables, with the weighting selected to minimise the regression error in the transformation to EWH. The observation-to-EWH transformation has also been improved, showing that the relationship is not only spatially variable but also time-dependent, reflecting changes in inter-satellite range and satellite altitude throughout the GRACE mission. These variations affect KBR sensitivity to mass change but should not appear as EWH variations; the updated transformation therefore accounts for these effects. The three formulations (range, LGD and hybrid) are available as 5-day EWH products (https://doi.org/10.4121/4fc748e8-01c7-4f06-87da-653937b078f7). 

Further developments include uncertainty propagation, which provides spatially and temporally resolved uncertainty estimates for the 5-day EWH fields. The additional uncertainty associated with reducing the temporal resolution from monthly to 5-day estimates remains moderate. Relative to the corresponding monthly solutions, the uncertainty increases by approximately 13–20% over land and 8–12% over the oceans. For comparison, reducing the averaging period from one month to five days while assuming independent observations and no additional information would yield an expected uncertainty increase of approximately 145%. The relatively small increase results from exploiting the spatial and temporal information contained in the KBR post-fit residuals rather than treating each 5-day solution as an independent gravity-field inversion. 

The approach does not use hydrological models or other external geophysical priors, nor does it require temporal regularisation or Kalman filtering. It therefore avoids the need for a separate high-frequency gravity inversion framework. The resulting 5-day EWH grids are evaluated against daily solutions and through case studies of the 2007 Bangladesh floods and the January 2013 Cyclone Oswald.

items.text: This study presents a methodological framework to temporally reconstruct and spatially downscale GRACE Terrestrial Water Storage (TWS) anomalies using a bias-aware Random Forest model for the transboundary Bug River Basin (Poland–Ukraine–Belarus). The approach incorporates three main innovations that enhance satellite-based TWS estimation. First, missing monthly TWS anomalies were reconstructed using an RF model driven solely by lagged GRACE values and calendar-month information, which avoided information leakage from auxiliary hydrological predictors and yielded a temporally continuous TWS record despite data gaps, including the 2017–2018 GRACE–GRACE-FO hiatus. Second, RF was used to downscale the reconstructed GRACE-derived TWS to a 0.1°×0.1° resolution, using precipitation, evapotranspiration, river runoff, and soil moisture as predictors, together with elevation, lithology, and land-cover class as static physiographic attributes. Third, a bias-aware, mass-conserving block-wise correction was applied to reconcile the downscaled fields with the original GRACE water mass at coarse resolution, by redistributing monthly systematic errors within spatial blocks using river-runoff-based weights, thereby enforcing exact mass-balance closure while preserving physically meaningful sub-grid variability.The results indicate that GRACE-derived TWS dynamics are best captured by a predictor with an integrated origin — river runoff — rather than by individual hydrometeorological drivers, underscoring the importance of multivariate approaches to downscaling. The combined use of hydrometeorological parameters allows the model to capture complementary aspects of the storage balance that are not evident from any single predictor alone. In terms of predictive skill, the 1-month lag dominates, consistent with strong month-to-month persistence in TWS. Month (the seasonal indicator) shows moderate importance. Among the independent predictors, hydrological variables were the dominant controls on the predicted GRACE-derived TWS values, with the three-month rolling mean of river runoff being the most influential predictor. The northern regions of the Bug River Basin exhibit stronger and more regular seasonal cycles, which enhances the effectiveness of the lagged predictors and seasonal encoding used in the imputation model. By contrast, the southern areas tend to show more episodic hydrological variability, potentially driven by localized precipitation extremes, rapid runoff responses, or human water management, which reduces temporal autocorrelation and limits predictability based solely on past GRACE observations. The spatial distribution of linear trends in GRACE-derived TWS reveals a coherent pattern of long-term storage decline over the full 2002–2024 period, with pronounced spatial heterogeneity: the magnitude of decline increases toward the southern part of the study area, where the strongest negative trends are observed.The proposed methodological framework, strengthened by rigorous spatiotemporal cross-validation and physically based mass-conservation constraints, enables improved monitoring and forecasting of groundwater in transboundary catchments and facilitates the reconstruction of continuous TWS changes over time and space, which is particularly valuable for regions with sparse or conflict-disrupted in-situ observation networks.

items.text: ONERA laboratory have been providing highly sensitive electrostatic accelerometers involved in all major space Geodesy missions for more than five decades. Since the first mission launched, the accuracy of the accelerometers has significantly improved over time. For instance, the ESA GOCE mission accelerometers exhibited a few 10-12ms-2Hz-1/2 resolution. In a Fundamental Physics application, the T-SAGE accelerometers developed at ONERA allowed to test the Equivalence Principle on board the MICROSCOPE satellite at a level of 10-15, establishing in 2022 the best accuracy ever achieved for the test, besting the previous one attained with Lunar Laser Ranging by two orders of magnitude.Currently, MicroSTAR accelerometers are selected for ESA Next Generation Gravity Mission (NGGM). This mission aims to extend observations provided by GRACE-family satellites, with the same strategy. ONERA’s project is ongoing and the instrument phase C started early 2026. Currently, the mechanical sensor reached TRL-6 while the electronic unit and the overall system achieved TRL-5 with a performance level foreseen of about a few 10-12ms-2Hz-1/2. In the same fashion as the past instruments, the accelerometer is based on the electrostatic suspension of a proof-mass. The position and the attitude of the mass are measured and controlled with capacitive sensors and actuators. One of the main improvements of MicroSTAR is its cubic proof-mass, as opposed to the previous parallelepipedal ones in SuperSTAR-type accelerometers, which allows a high accuracy measurement along and around all three axes.To reach the technical and performance needs of NGGM, improvements in all technological fields are fundamental. In this presentation, the current development of MicroSTAR with its challenges and key strengths will be presented.

items.title: Mass column height determined from a TVG field by inversion in the spatial domain
items.authors: Josef Sebera and Aleš Bezděk

affiliations.text: Astronomical Institute, ASCR, CZ Astronomical Institute, ASCR, CZ

items.text: Time-variable gravity (TVG) fields from satellite gravimetry missions deliver water column height by employing the spectral approach that relates the gravitational potential and the mass column height (i.e., equivalent water height, EWH). Such EWH can be rescaled at a later stage by a density ratio to adapt the column heights to a lateral density variation. Mass column height is important when satellite gravimetry products are combined/compared with geometrical techniques such as satellite altimetry. Checking this rescaling is thus desirable as the gravimetry and altimetry can only be put together by appropriate density modelling (apart from other questions such as temporal and spatial resolution etc.). Validation of the spectral approach and the rescaling can be done only by an independent approach. In our contribution, we show that it can be done by inverting TVG fields in the spatial domain if necessary corrections are also applied in the spatial domain. The spectral and spatial approaches for estimating mass column height differ in many respects, each offers certain pros and cons, e.g. the spectral approach is very time effective while the spatial one offers a certain degree of freedom in its setup. The numerical examples are shown for Greenland where the TVG signal (e.g., the trend) is known to be largest and where the satellite altimetry is used with the GRACE and GRACE-FO data products.

items.text: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major component of the climate system, redistributing heat, freshwater and carbon through the Atlantic. Although substantial weakening is projected under continued climate change, the magnitude and timing of future change remain uncertain. Detecting a sustained anthropogenic trend is particularly difficult because direct observations are spatially limited and short relative to the AMOC’s strong natural variability. Satellite gravimetry offers a complementary observing strategy because AMOC variability produces a characteristic ocean-bottom-pressure (OBP) signal across the western boundary of the North Atlantic. However, the narrow cross-slope scale of this signal, together with measurement noise and leakage from continental hydrology, presents a demanding observational challenge. We assess the feasibility of recovering AMOC variability and long-term change using simulated gravimetry observations. Monthly output from a 1/12° North Atlantic ocean model is used to establish the relationship between AMOC transport and OBP over the upper and lower continental slope. Modelled OBP fields are transformed into spherical harmonics and progressively truncated to quantify the effects of limited spatial resolution. We then apply simulated mission errors and filtering representative of GRACE-C-like, Next Generation Gravity Mission (NGGM) and MAGIC configurations. Spherical-harmonic truncation substantially attenuates the narrow western-boundary OBP signals, but their cross-slope contrast, and hence the associated AMOC variability, remains recoverable at resolutions achievable by future missions. The most robust estimate is obtained from the difference between lower- and upper-slope OBP averaged over carefully selected latitude ranges. GRACE-C-like errors are generally too large for reliable recovery, whereas NGGM and MAGIC reproduce much of the modelled interannual-to-decadal variability; MAGIC provides a smaller additional improvement over NGGM alone. Sustained trends are also recoverable over plausible mission lifetimes, with trend uncertainties of approximately 0.8 Sv decade⁻¹ and weakening rates of around 2 Sv decade⁻¹ or greater becoming detectable in the simulations. These results demonstrate that next-generation satellite gravimetry could provide basin-scale monitoring of AMOC variability and emerging trends, complementing sustained in-situ arrays and extending observations beyond a single latitude.

items.authors: Roelof Rietbroek and Sedigheh Karimi

affiliations.text: University of Twente, Faculty of Geo-information and Earth Observation, Enschede, Netherlands University of Twente, Faculty of Geo-information and Earth Observation, Enschede, Netherlands

items.text:
The spurious North-South stripes in gravity field solutions of satellite gravimetry mission such as GRACE and its follow-on (GRACE-FO), are a well known issue. They are thought to be the result of residual non-Gaussian errors, most notably stemming from residual sub-monthly dealiasing model errors, which propagate into the gravity field solutions. The typical pattern is known to be linked to the orbit geometry (e.g. Peidou and Pagiatakis 2020) in combination with the directional sensitivity of the raw observations.

Over the years, various approaches have been developed to reduce these striping patterns as a trade-off against signal attenuation, resulting in varying filtered solutions. One particular type of these approaches stems from using diagonal regularization matrices using approximate or real error-covariance matrices (e.g. Kusche et al 2009, Klees et al 2008, Horvath et al. 2018). These can be done either at the normal equation system level or be formulated as a post-processing filter operator.

In this work, we revisit this regularization principle and explore ways of constraining the East-West and North-South gravity field gradients at given satellite heights.
We show that, in the spherical harmonic domain, the associated regularization matrices resolve to order-block-diagonal matrices with a typical checkerboard pattern separating even and odd degrees. 
Furthermore, we compute an empirical degree varying power law for the gradients based on the ESA earth system model (Dobslaw et al 2015). We present the result of testing various regularization strengths and weighing schemes, which are applied to the publicly available normal equation system from ITSG. The regularized solutions are compared against conventional filter approaches (DDK filters, Gauss,) in the spatial and spectral domain.

items.text: Satellite laser ranging (SLR) tracking data is routinely used to determine low-degree time-variable gravity fields, typically to maximum degrees/orders ranging from 5 to 10. Several methods have been developed to combine the longer and continuous record of SLR and the significantly better spatial resolution and accuracy of the GRACE and GRACE-FO fields to construct gap-free mass change estimates starting in 1993 (or earlier), each with their own limitations and assumptions. Our group has previously shown that large-scale regularized mascons can be estimated from SLR tracking data, while also noting that these initial solutions exhibited high sensitivity to the regularization design. Here we present a new set of large global mascons derived from regularized SLR inversions, where the regularization matrices (diagonal signal covariance matrices centered on a zero state) have been optimized using a simple genetic algorithm. The performance metric (i.e., fitness) of each randomized mutation is defined as the misfit between the de-trended SLR and GRACE/-FO solutions, noting that at these large spatial scales GRACE/-FO mass changes can safely be treated as the truth. This work results in a unique continuous time series of global mass change, including degree 1, from 1993 to the present. We compare our results to GRACE/-FO regional mass change and to IMBIE assessments of ice sheet mass change.

items.authors: Felipe Guzman and Jose Sanjuan

items.text: ODIN and THOR represent two complementary advances in low-frequency optomechanical inertial sensing aimed at enabling next-generation mass change missions. ODIN, the Optomechanical Distributed Instrument for Inertial Sensing and Navigation, is a compact, low-cost, and power-efficient system currently supported by NASA's InVEST program and manifested for flight on the GRATTIS mission in February 2027. It consists of an array of linear accelerometers capable of high-precision inertial measurements below 10⁻⁹ m s⁻²/√Hz, with angular sensitivities better than 50 μrad/√Hz. Laboratory demonstrations have reached noise floors below 8 pico-g above 60 mHz, positioning ODIN as a strong candidate for mass change studies, inertial navigation in GPS-denied environments, and planetary seismology, where size, weight, and power constraints dominate.THOR, the Triaxial High-sensitivity Optomechanical Reference, builds directly on ODIN heritage and is aimed at maturing optomechanical triaxial sensing technologies for spaceborne mass change observations. THOR targets linear acceleration sensitivities of 10⁻⁹ m s⁻²/√Hz along three orthogonal axes across a measurement bandwidth of 1–100 mHz.Together, ODIN and THOR advance optomechanical inertial sensing toward higher technology readiness, offering reduced cost, size, weight, and power, an innovative alternative to electrostatic systems, and support for flexible mission architectures. I will present the current status of these two spaceflight instruments.
