items.title: Deployment of a Long-Term Self-Calibrating Ocean Bottom Pressure Recorder in the Nordic Seas for GRACE-FO, GRACE-C, and NGGM Validation
items.authors: Cecilia Peralta-Ferriz, John Guthrie, and James Morison

affiliations.text: Applied Physics Laboratory, University of Washington, Seattle, USA Applied Physics Laboratory, University of Washington, Seattle, USA

items.text: We report the successful deployment of a Sonardyne Fetch AZA ocean bottom pressure recorder at the Oceanographic Weather Station M (66°N, 2°E) in the Nordic Seas in June 2026. The deployment and data recovery efforts are supported by NASA's GRACE-FO Science Team and the University of Bergen, with the goal of providing an independent, long-term in situ record for the validation and interpretation of satellite gravimetry observations. The instrument was deployed at approximately 2,034 m depth, about 2 km west of the long-term physical oceanographic mooring at Station M, and is recording hourly ocean bottom pressure and temperature. The instrument is equipped with batteries designed to support up to 10 years of operation and an acoustic transducer that enables data to be retrieved remotely from the surface without recovering or disturbing the instrument on the seafloor. A key capability of the Fetch AZA is its in situ self-calibration system, which enables characterization and correction of long-term pressure-sensor drift – a major limitation of conventional bottom pressure records for resolving low-frequency ocean mass variability. An initial data harvest approximately 11 hours after deployment successfully recovered the first measurements and confirmed proper instrument operation. Strong acoustic communications were also established from multiple ranging locations approximately 1 km from the triangulated instrument position, demonstrating the feasibility of future acoustic data recovery. Annual data recovery is planned to build a multi-year, drift-corrected ocean bottom pressure record for comparison with GRACE-FO and future GRACE-C and NGGM observations, and for validation and improvement of their data products.

items.title: Enhanced Retrieval of the Seasonal Cycle of Terrestrial Water Storage
items.authors: Matthew Rodell1, Mary Michael O'Neill1,2, and Bryant Loomis1

affiliations.text: Earth Sciences Division, NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA

items.text: Standard spherical harmonic and mascon approaches can attenuate mass change signals. Among other effects, this leads to mischaracterization of the seasonal cycle of terrestrial water storage (TWS), spatially smoothing and underestimating the peak amplitude in particular. When GRACE/FO derived TWS is included in a water budget analysis, that underestimation leads to a mismatch with the accumulated fluxes of precipitation, evapotranspiration, and runoff. Herein we present results of a new approach to deriving the seasonal cycle of TWS, which relies on L1B data stacking. We show that the new technique better retains the amplitude of the seasonal signal, making it more appropriate for use in water budget analyses.

items.text: The central hypothesis of the Research Unit (RU) New Refined Observations of Climate Change from Spaceborne Gravity Missions (NEROGRAV) reads: only by concurrently improving and better understanding of sensor data, background models, and processing strategies of satellite gravimetry, the resolution, accuracy, and long-term consistency of mass transport series from satellite gravimetry can be significantly increased; and only in that case, the potential of future technological sensor developments can be fully exploited.In continuation of the first RU phase, the individual project Improved Stochastic Modeling in GRACE/GRACE-FO Real Data Processing (ISTORE-2) aims to complete the optimized stochastic modeling for GRACE and GRACE-FO gravity field determination. This includes stochastic modeling of the non-tidal atmospheric and oceanic dealiasing (AOD) models which were recently implemented into the GRACE/GRACE-FO Level-2 processing at the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences. In this context, we co-estimate AOD model coefficients using AOD error variance-covariance matrices (VCMs) in terms of constraint matrices.This presentation provides an overview of the main processing steps together with AOD error analyses. In particular, we investigate the impact of taking into account not only stationary but also non-stationary AOD VCMs. Results are presented in terms of gravity field solutions in the spectral and spatial domain.

items.title: Ground experiment to study the interaction of a bounded plasma with a metal shield
items.authors: Anja Schlicht

affiliations.text: TU Munich, FESG, Munich, Germany TU Munich, FESG, Munich, Germany

items.text: Unknown effects heavily disturb space accelerometers of gravity field missions. Disturbances in GRACE called twangs could be related to excitations in the ionosphere. This motivated the study of possible interaction between the ionosphere and space instruments. We report on a ground experiment conducted in a plasma chamber, where we reproduced the switching of heaters and the reaction of a shielded and un-shielded receiving antenna. We identified the signature of plasma excitations as typical for a bounded plasma in a cavity, where a neutral layer establishes between the metal surface and the plasma. In addition, we see excitations of smaller frequencies, which would fit to mechanical resonances of the metal shield. The plasma excitations could be shielded, whereas the lower frequencies stay in the response of the receiver. Beneath the presentation of the experiment, we will propose a possible mechanism for the excitation of mechanical resonances of metals by plasma waves disturbing the layer between a metal and a plasma.

items.title: The Response of GRACE/GRACE-FO to 14,000 Global Lakes from 1992 to 2026
items.authors: Kevin Gaastra, Donald Argus, Felix Landerer, David Wiese, and Athina Peidou

affiliations.text: Jet Propulsion Laboratory Jet Propulsion Laboratory

items.text: We estimate changes in lake levels and volumes from October 1992 to April 2026 each month for 14,071 natural lakes and artificial reservoirs larger than 10 km2 contained within the surface water and ocean topography (SWOT) mission’s prior lake database (PLD). We use altimetric lake level estimates from G-REALM, DAHITI, HydroWeb, the SWOT mission, and the Global Lake Water Storage dataset’s hypsometric relationships to establish a complete timeseries of lake water storage over the study interval interpolating and extrapolating a seasonal where data is missing. From this information we construct three data products to disaggregate global lake water from GRACE terrestrial water storage: 1) timeseries of lake level and storage over the study interval, 2) maps of change in lake water for the 11,386 natural lakes and 2,685 artificial reservoirs on a 16th degree global grid each month, 3) lake-generated changes in equivalent water thickness as seen by GRACE for both JPL’s 3-degree mascon solution and for the spherical harmonic solutions of GRACE. Of the 1706 3-degree terrestrial mascons 1109 (65%) are affected by lake water; 808 mascons (73%) experience a decrease in weighted root mean square (WRMS) when lake water is removed, while 301 mascons (27%) experience an increase in WRMS. This dataset shows a 14-fold increase in the number of lakes studied compared to our previous lake model as well as an extension to 2026 (Gaastra et al. 2025). Correspondingly the number of mascons affected roughly doubles and the percentage of mascons experiencing an increase in WRMS has increased as coverage of high latitude lakes is improved. High latitude and high elevation regions experience an increase in WRMS when lake water is removed primarily due to glacial and snow melt fed lakes which experience their maximum seasonal water during the summers when terrestrial water storage is low as snow has melted. We find the regions where lake water disagrees substantially with GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water are mainly concentrated in high latitude regions, alpine regions, and arid near costal mascons.

items.title: Quantifying total drainable water storage and its distribution using GRACE/GRACE-FO

items.text: Total Drainable Water Storage (TDWS) is the portion of basin water storage that can be released through drainage and sustain river discharge. River discharge has intrinsic environmental value, as it provides the water needed to sustain river ecosystems, particularly during dry periods. A consistent global estimate of TDWS would therefore provide a new basis for comparing the capacity of river basins to sustain discharge and for identifying regions with comparatively limited drainable water-storage capacity. Despite its hydrological relevance, TDWS has not yet been estimated at the global scale from satellite gravimetry observations. As demonstrated in previous studies, TDWS can be inferred by linking temporal variations in basin water storage to river discharge through a runoff–storage relationship. GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE/GRACE-FO) provide a unique observational basis for this purpose by measuring Terrestrial Water Storage Anomalies (TWSA) across large river basins worldwide. However, TWSA includes storage components with different timing and routing characteristics relative to river discharge, which can introduce phase shifts and hysteresis into the storage–discharge relationship. We therefore derive Drainable Water Storage Anomalies (DWSA) by accounting separately for snow, lake, wetland, and reservoir storage. The resulting DWSA time series are combined with monthly river discharge observations from the Global Runoff Data Centre (GRDC) to characterize the runoff–storage relationship and estimate both TDWS and the characteristic drainage time, representing the timescale over which drainable storage is released through river discharge. Here, we provide the first global basin-scale quantification of TDWS from GRACE/GRACE-FO observations by applying this framework to more than 200 globally distributed river basins using three independent GRACE/GRACE-FO mascon solutions from CSR, JPL, and GSFC. Basin-scale TWSA and the corresponding DWSA are derived independently for each mascon product, enabling us to assess the consistency and robustness of TDWS and drainage-time estimates with respect to differences in gravity-field processing. We further examine the global spatial variability of both quantities and evaluate the suitability of the runoff–storage relationship for individual basins. This evaluation is important because uncertainties in river discharge, and weak or nonlinear storage–discharge behavior can affect the reliability of the inferred basin parameters. Together, TDWS and characteristic drainage time provide complementary information on how much water a basin can release through drainage and the timescale over which this storage is discharged. Their global estimation enables a consistent comparison of drainage behavior across river basins and helps identify differences in their capacity to sustain river flow during periods without precipitation.

items.title: GRACE/GRACE-FO radio occultations for weather forecast and climate research
items.authors: Torsten Schmidt, Patrick Schreiner, and Jens Wickert

items.text: The major objective of the GRACE Follow On (GFO) mission with its two satellites GF1 and GF2 is to obtain precise global and high-resolution models for both the static and the time variable components of the Earth's gravity field. Additional goal is the continuation of the GPS radio occultation (RO) measurements from the predecessor GRACE, successfully performed between 2006 and 2017.Starting with the CHAMP mission, the GFZ has been continuously processing radio occultation data since 2001 and has been providing it operationally in near real time to weather services since 2006. GFZ RO data, as GRACE and GFO also contribute to the global RO data base for climate research.Following the successful RO missions CHAMP (2001–2008) and GRACE (2006–2017), the GFZ is currently still processing RO data from TerraSAR-X (since 2008), Tandem-X (since 2011), and the two GRACE-FO satellites (since 2020), with TerraSAR-X representing the longest continuous RO data set to date. The complete RO data set has been reprocessed since 2026.In this presentation, we discuss climatologies and temperature trends in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (5-40 km) and tropopause parameters derived from the GFZ data set (2002-2025) and compare the results with UCAR and ERA5 data. The importance of smaller RO missions for weather and climate research is emphasized.

items.text: Recent advances in optical clock technology offer the possibility of directly sensing differences in the Earth’s gravitational potential through frequency comparisons between satellites. This study investigates the performance of different satellite formation-flying architectures for recovering the time-variable gravity field using optical clock measurements.Four formation geometries are considered: a GRACE-like along-track configuration and three multidirectional formations, namely Cartwheel, Pendulum, and Helix. We performed a simulation analysis over 2016-2018 and synthesized the observable, geopotential difference, based on Hydrology, Icesheet and Solid Earth components of the v3 of the ESA Earth System Model. The observations were then contaminated with AOD1B error (from AOe07) and various clock noise levels from 10-17 to 10-20. We estimated monthly spherical harmonic solutions to degree 60, and evaluated the results in the spectral and spatial domain, as well as through examining timeseries of terrestrial water storage changes and icesheet mass change. The results show that formation geometry strongly influences the quality and spatial characteristics of time-variable gravity solutions. Our results show that a clock noise level of 10-19-10-20 is required to reliably recover time-variable gravity fields. Compared with the GRACE-like formation, multidirectional formations such as the Pendulum provide substantially improved solutions, both in terms of error magnitude and isotropy, making the errors easier to mitigate with a simple Gaussian filter. The performance of formation-flying missions depends strongly on clock noise, highlighting an important interplay between measurement precision and formation geometry. As clock performance improves, the influence of constellation geometry becomes increasingly important, with the Pendulum and Helix configurations showing particularly promising time-variable gravity recovery capabilities, especially at smaller spatial scales.

items.text: Monthly gravity-field solutions derived from satellite laser ranging (SLR) and Doppler Orbitography and Radiopositioning Integrated by Satellite (DORIS) provide an observational record that extends well before the GRACE era but resolve only a limited range of spatial wavelengths. In this study, we implement deep learning methods to generate monthly gravity fields up to degree 60 from SLR/DORIS products (up to degree 10) by targeting COST-G GRACE(-FO) solutions. items.text: Despite improvements from the GOT5.6 ocean tide model adopted for RL07 processing, tide model error remains a significant source of temporal aliasing in GRACE gravimetry. This effect is felt particularly in shallow shelves with complex bathymetry and a larger than normal presence of nonlinear tides, as well as in regions where hydrodynamic models are least constrained by observations. The cornerstone altimetry missions used to constrain modern tide models rely on an open surface and are inclined at around 66 degrees, limiting their coverage and leaving high latitudes constrained primarily by in-situ measurements, high-inclination altimetry and hydrodynamic models. SWOT extends coverage to 78 degrees latitude, but remains dependent on an open surface and its record since 2022 falls short of separating several closely spaced tidal constituents. GRACE and GRACE-FO have effectively global coverage, an extended time series history, and observe mass distribution rather than surface level, making them uniquely suitable for tidal estimation in high-latitude and ice-covered regions despite GRACE's relatively poor spatial resolution.We utilize a localized formulation following Han et al. (2008) to estimate residual mass anomalies and tides from GRACE inter-satellite range-rate residuals. Surface mass is parameterized as equivalent water height on a regional grid, gravitational acceleration is calculated by point-mass approximation and integrated along the nominal orbits, and mass anomaly and tidal signals are recovered relative to the CSR background gravity field and ocean tide model. Per-pass state deviation vectors are estimated to absorb out-of-region errors, long wavelength orbit signals, and accelerometer errors. The temporal basis is evaluated at each observation epoch, allowing for simultaneous estimation of sub-daily tidal harmonic signals alongside mean mass anomalies over arbitrary averaging intervals and reducing the leakage of non-tidal signals into the tidal residual estimates.The regional mass anomaly inversion of GRACE residuals is ill-posed and requires an extensive regularization scheme to produce meaningful results. Range-rate data constrain an along-track projection of the mass field, and arc state deviation parameters often compete with the mass anomaly parameters for the same long-wavelength signals. We discuss the conditioning of the problem, the regularization strategies that yielded a stable solution in the current model, and the sensitivity of the recovered field to regularization weights.Validation of the current model against CSR global solutions for monthly mean mass anomalies confirms the estimator geometry, regularization, and arc parameterization. items.text: Observations of mass changes in the cryosphere are critical to understanding the impact of climate change and constraining global projections of sea-level rise. Observations from satellite gravimetry missions, satellite altimetry, and Surface Mass Balance (SMB) models provide differing estimates of mass change at different temporal and spatial scales making intercomparison challenging. GRACE-FO is equipped with two sensors to track the inter-satellite distance; a baseline K-band microwave ranging system (KBR) and an experimental Laser Ranging Interferometer (LRI). The improved ranging precision of the LRI enables Line-of-Sight Gravity Difference (LGD) observations with substantially greater sensitivity to short-wavelength gravity signals than is possible with the KBR and at a range of temporal scales. Building on previous work demonstrating enhanced high-frequency sensitivity over Greenland and Antarctica, we apply LGD as a validation tool for GRACE-FO mascon products, ICESat-2-derived mass-change estimates, and two versions of the RACMO SMB model over the same region. This tests products commonly used for mass-change observations in the cryosphere over a range of spatial and temporal scales. LRI-derived LGD uniquely enables an independent direct frequency domain validation of the effective gravity signals from different mas change products without the limiting effects of temporal aliasing. By forward modeling gravity from monthly mass-change solutions and comparing the resulting synthetic LGD with LRI LGD observations, we assess the ability of different mass-change products to recover signals over multiple spatial and temporal scales. The results demonstrate that the effective spatial resolution of mass-change products is not characterized by a single spatial scale but instead depends on the interaction between the magnitude of the mass-change signal, the spatial and temporal scale of mass changes, and the measurement or modeling technique. This validation is particularly important for the cryosphere where understanding the effective spatial and temporal resolution of products can change the interpretation of the data. Validation of mass-change products using LGD provides a new approach for evaluating existing mass-change products in Greenland and Antarctica as well as guiding the development of future mass-change products.

items.title: Assessing Machine Learning for Automated Screening of GRACE-C Quicklook Gravity Solutions

affiliations.text: University of Texas, Center for Space Research, United States of America University of Texas, Center for Space Research, United States of America

items.text:
Scheduled for launch in 2028, GRACE-C is expected to provide Quicklook gravity field solutions
with a latency of approximately three days. Such low latency necessitates an operational
validation schedule best suited to automated or semi-automated frameworks. Machine learning
(ML) offers the potential for rapid, automated quality screening of solutions as "physically
consistent," "sub-optimal," or "anomalous." However, predicting Liquid Water Equivalent (LWE)
values at the per-pixel level is challenging given the limited 241-month time series and the
complex spatial, temporal, annual, and spherical correlations within the data. Additionally,
month-to-month LWE variability increases throughout time, indicating increasingly dynamic
hydrological signals across the GRACE and GRACE-FO eras.

To investigate the feasibility of ML to support automated validation of GRACE-C Quicklook
solutions, we systematically compared a diverse set of ML architectures including regularized
linear models, tree-based ensembles, spatiotemporal dimensionality-reduction techniques, and
deep neural networks. Model skill is then assessed relative to a per-pixel persistence baseline,
providing a consistent reference for determining actual predictive skill. We further examine the
sensitivity of model performance to hyperparameters and feature selection through systematic
spatiotemporal ablation experiments, with particular attention to the characteristics of GRACE-
derived signals. Hydro-meteorological variables are evaluated across a range of climatic
domains to characterize their predictive value. We have currently enacted a 5-fold temporal
cross-validation with overlap purging alongside basin-level spatial folds to prevent data leakage
and spatial-temporal memorization. These experiments provide an initial assessment of the
range of useful architecture and features that may serve a physically informed approach to
screening GRACE-C Quicklook solutions.

items.title: Seismic Effects of Large Earthquakes on Sea‐Level Budget Closures
items.authors: Tony Song1, Felix Landerer1, Benjamin Hamlington1, Hyeonsoo Cha2, and Jae-Hong Moon2

affiliations.text: Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, United States of America
Jeju National University, South Korea

items.text: Large undersea earthquakes can distort ocean bottom pressure (OBP) measurements from the GRACE and GRACE-FO satellites, making it difficult to close regional sea-level budgets in earthquake-prone areas. In this talk, we will show that these earthquake-related signals can be effectively removed using an iterative Empirical Orthogonal Function (EOF) method that captures both sudden co-seismic changes and longer-lasting post-seismic effects. The results demonstrate that these seismic signals are non-negligible and introduce a systematic bias associated with ongoing tectonic motion. In some regions, this bias can exceed sea-level changes caused by ocean warming (steric effects), while globally it can even exceed the signal expected from Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA). These findings highlight the importance of accounting for seismic effects when assessing regional and global sea-level budgets and separating natural and anthropogenic contributions to observed climate change.

items.title: Sub-monthly Terrestrial Water Storage Change from GRACE-C and NGGM: Assessing MAGIC’s Capability for Rapid Mass Change Monitoring
items.authors: Khosro Ghobadi-Far

affiliations.text: University of Colorado Boulder, Department of Aerospace Engineering Sciences, United States of America University of Colorado Boulder, Department of Aerospace Engineering Sciences, United States of America

items.text: By mitigating temporal aliasing errors caused by unresolved high-frequency atmospheric and oceanic mass variations, MAGIC is expected to provide substantially improved estimates of terrestrial water storage (TWS) changes. To date, MAGIC's performance has been evaluated primarily using global gravity field inversions. In this presentation, I evaluate its performance using the Line-of-sight Gravity Difference (LGD) approach, with a particular focus on addressing two major limitations of the current GRACE/-FO missions for terrestrial hydrology: their coarse spatial resolution of ~300 km and monthly temporal sampling, which limit their ability to monitor rapidly evolving events such as floods. To this end, I perform a regional inversion of sub-monthly (10-day) surface water storage changes over the Amazon Basin. The Amazon's large-amplitude, localized hydrologic signals and rapid sub-monthly variability provide an ideal test case for evaluating spatial resolutions finer than the ~300 km achievable with monthly GRACE/-FO solutions. The results show that, for 10-day TWS change solutions, GRACE-C and NGGM achieve comparable performance at a spatial scale of 330 km, whereas NGGM outperforms GRACE-C at 220 km and 165 km. NGGM recovers approximately 80% and 65% of the 10-day TWS signal at spatial scales of 220 km and 165 km, respectively, representing a 15-20% improvement over GRACE-C. I also quantify the effects of orbital geometry (i.e., the inclined orbit) and altitude on NGGM’s improved results. Between latitudes ±70°, the improved performance of MAGIC is largely driven by the contribution of the inclined NGGM pair. These results demonstrate the potential of MAGIC to substantially advance spatiotemporal monitoring of TWS change and enable observations of hydrologic processes at spatial and temporal scales beyond the capabilities of the current GRACE/-FO missions.

items.title: Is the contribution of glaciers and ice sheets to sea level rise slowing down?
items.authors: Isabella Velicogna1,2, Arnav Agrawal1, Tyler Sutterley3, and Geruo Aa1

items.text: We report on the ice mass loss of the Antarctic and Greenland Icesheets and of the world Glaciers and ice caps from 2002 to 2026 using data from the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) missions.In Greenland, we detect a slowdown in ice mass loss since 2012 due to lower melt runoff production caused by a succession of colder summers, especially in the southwest and northeast sectors. The mass loss averages 245+/-47 Gt/year for the period 2002-2026 with the acceleration in loss negligible after 2012 due to reduced surface melt, especially in the southwest and northeast. A disproportionate portion of the mass loss is driven by North Greenland which includes the two largest marine-based basins, which are most prone to rapid sea level rise.In Antarctica, we detect a slowdown in ice mass loss in 2019-2024 which was caused by an increase in accumulation of snowfall, especially in Queen Maud Land, which is unprecedented in the GRACE record. Increase in snowfall is also observed in Totem and Moscow and Wilkins land East Antarctica and in the Antarctic Peninsula. This short-lived mass gain in 2019-2024 mirrors a similar episode in 2004–2007 both in magnitude and duration, reflecting interannual variability in surface mass balance, not a reversal of long-term trends. A disproportionate portion of the mass loss is controlled by the Amundsen Sea Embayment of West Antarctica and to a lesser extent by the Wilkes Land sector of East Antarctica. Both ice sheets continue to lose ice, with no statistically significant acceleration during the GRACE era, confirming that Antarctica’s apparent recovery is a brief snowfall-driven pause within a persistent long-term decline.For the world Glacial and Ice Caps (GIC) we find a sustained mass loss of 296+/-30 Gt/year and an acceleration in mass loss of 6+/-2 Gt/year^2, the Arctic is still dominating the GIC mass loss signal and account for 71% of the total GIC mass loss. Ice sheet and Glaciers continue to have a major impact on sea level rise, the ice sheets show a relative loss in acceleration after 2012, but the longer record 1979-2025 shows an acceleration in mass loss.

items.text: Groundwater is a critical component of water supply across the Colorado River Basin (CRB), particularly during prolonged surface-water shortages. We use GRACE/FO satellite gravimetry together with complementary hydrologic datasets to assess groundwater-storage variability across the Upper and Lower CRB from 2004 to 2023 and to quantify relationships between groundwater drought and surface-water deficits.The satellite record shows persistent groundwater depletion across the basin, with losses accelerating after 2019 and during the 2020–2022 drought. During this period, groundwater losses reached 17.5 ± 3.5 km³ in the Upper CRB, exceeding the 9.4 ± 6.5 km³ lost in the Lower CRB despite the Upper Basin’s typically greater hydrologic resilience.Copula-based modeling combined with statistical inference further reveals contrasting groundwater–surface water relationships between the two subbasins. In the Upper CRB, groundwater drought probability increases strongly with surface-water deficits and exceeds 60% under moderate shortages. In contrast, parts of the Lower CRB show weaker statistical dependence, consistent with groundwater extraction operating partly independently of short-term surface-water availability under chronically limited supply.These results highlight distinct regional controls on groundwater vulnerability across the CRB and demonstrate the value of GRACE-based monitoring combined with probabilistic statistical approaches for quantifying the likelihood of groundwater drought under surface-water stress.

items.text: Global ocean mass change is a major driver of present-day global mean sea level (GMSL) rise and a key indicator of climate change. Over the past three decades, mass loss from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets has been a major contributor to global ocean mass change. Since 2002, GRACE/-FO has provided invaluable observations of ice-sheet and ocean mass changes, whereas direct observations remain limited for the pre-GRACE era. Here, we use time-variable gravity fields derived from GRACE/-FO, satellite laser ranging (SLR) and Doppler Orbitography and Radiopositioning Integrated by Satellite (DORIS) to estimate long-term mass changes in the global ocean and ice sheets since 1993, the beginning of the high-precision satellite altimetry era. Major challenges associated with signal leakage and geocenter motion are addressed using a global forward-modeling technique. Using these satellite-gravimetry-based estimates, we reconcile the GMSL budget and compare ice sheet mass changes with estimates from independent techniques. Our results demonstrate the added value of SLR and DORIS observations in complementing the GRACE/-FO record and highlight the importance of further investigations into historical satellite gravimetry data to improve estimates of long-term mass changes in the Earth system.

items.text:
Space gravimetry from GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE/GRACE-FO; GGFO)
provides quasi-monthly estimates of global mass redistribution that can
be mapped into elastic surface displacements. Although spatially coarser
than the station-based observations underpinning terrestrial reference frame
solutions, GGFO-derived displacements show substantial consistency with GNSS
estimates, particularly in the vertical component, where correlations with
IGS Repro3 solutions approach 0.7 for both CSR and JPL mascon products. This
complementarity offers an opportunity to improve the representation of
non-tidal surface deformation in terrestrial reference frame (TRF) solutions.JPL TRF products are generated using a square-root information Kalman filter
that assimilates product-level inputs from GNSS, VLBI, SLR, and DORIS within
a common state-space framework. In JTRF2020 and subsequent realizations,
non-tidal loading is represented primarily through co-estimated seasonal and
other temporal components. Here we investigate an alternative formulation in
which GGFO-inferred deformation is introduced as an exogenous control input
driving the load-responsive components of the TRF state, so that gravimetry
contributes to state evolution rather than entering as an additional
observation equation.Starting from Level-3 mascon solutions, surface mass fields are transformed
into the spherical-harmonic domain and adjusted to obtain a consistent
representation of time-variable gravity, including treatment of degree-1
and other low-degree coefficients, model-dependent corrections, and removed
and restored non-tidal geophysical variability. The framework can also
operate directly on conventional spherical-harmonic gravity solutions. Gaps
in monthly geopotential-coefficient time series are reconstructed using
multichannel singular spectrum analysis (MSSA), followed by interpolation
to daily cadence using piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation. The resulting
daily fields are converted to elastic surface displacements using load Love

items.text: Temporal aliasing artefacts arising from unaccounted high-frequency mass variations in the geophysical fluid layers of the Earth are one of the most important error sources in present-day GRACE/-FO monthly-mean gravity field time-series. For the hydrological mass signal, we use sub-monthly TWS output from the recently improved open-source global hydrological model OS LISFLOOD, which we introduce into the ITSG-Grace processing scheme operated at TU Graz. We evaluate the effects of (i) deterministic information about TWS variability only, and (ii) additionally stochastic information on the remaining uncertainties in the modelled TWS data, which are obtained by performing a small ensemble of OS LISFLOOD model runs forced with different atmospheric reanalysis data.Even though temporal aliasing artefacts associated with TWS variability are substantially smaller than those originating from atmosphere and ocean, we conclude that the incorporation of hydrological background model information as derived from OS LISFLOOD into GRACE/-FO processing is advantageous for the quality of monthly solutions and should be considered to be included into the next major reprocessing of the satellite data record. items.text: he ESA Earth System Model (ESA ESM) provides a synthetic data set of the time-variable global gravity field that includes realistic mass variations in atmosphere, oceans, terrestrial water storage, continental ice sheets, and the solid Earth on a wide range of spatial and temporal frequencies. For more than 10 years already, it is widely applied as a source model in end-to-end simulation studies for future gravity missions, but has been also utilized to study novel gravity observing concepts on the ground. For those purposes, the ESM needs to include a wide range of signals even at very small spatial scales which might not yet have been reliably observed by any active satellite mission.In this contribution, we present the details of the newly released version 3.0 of the ESA ESM as well as the first simulation studies based on the new model. The changes to the previous ESA ESM version 2 include the utilization of a small ensemble of co- and post-seismic earthquake signals, an updated GIA model, additional mass balance signals from previously not considered Arctic glaciers, sub-monthly surface-mass balance changes and a more realistic representation of ice sheet dynamics. Extreme hydrometeorological events as well as climate-driven and anthropogenic impacts on continental water storage are represented through an update of the hydrological component. Additionally, the ESM separately includes ocean bottom pressure variations along the western slope of the Atlantic, representing variations in the meridional overturning circulation as a critically important component of the interactively coupled global climate system. ESA ESM 3.0 is available with 6-hour resolution from January 2007 until December 2020. It is augmented with synthetic error time series for atmosphere and ocean as well as hydrology to facilitate stochastical modelling of residual background model errors.

items.text:
GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) provide the primary satellite gravimetry observations of terrestrial water storage (TWS) variations from 2002 onwards. However, continuously improving global hydrological models often span substantially longer periods, while their validation in the pre-GRACE era remains challenging and requires complementary observations or long-term gravity field reconstructions. The validation can be conducted by combining information from GRACE with other geodetic techniques, such as Satellite Laser Ranging (SLR) and Doppler Orbitography and Radiopositioning Integrated by Satellite (DORIS). An important question, however, is to what extent hydrological model assessments depend on the choice of long-term gravity field reconstruction used as a benchmark.To address this question, we use our recently developed long-term SLR+GRACE gravity field reconstruction, which extends GRACE information back to 1995 by combining the complementary strengths of SLR and GRACE. The lowest-degree spherical harmonics are constrained directly by SLR, while intermediate and higher degrees incorporate GRACE-derived temporal and spatial information to provide gravity field solutions up to degree and order 60 also for the pre-GRACE period. 
We compare this reconstruction with an independently developed SLR+DORIS gravity field solution over the common period 1995–2022. Their applicability as long-term hydrological benchmarks is evaluated for the 100 largest river basins using TWS estimates from OS LISFLOOD and the Land Surface Discharge Model (LSDM), which has been widely used in geodetic applications for nearly two decades. Model benchmark agreement is quantified using the centered Kling–Gupta Efficiency (cKGE) and Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE). In addition, differences in NSE between OS LISFLOOD and LSDM (ΔNSE) are compared between the SLR+GRACE and SLR+DORIS benchmarks to assess whether both gravity field reconstructions lead to the same qualitative ranking of the hydrological models.The results show that OS LISFLOOD is generally more consistent with the gravimetric benchmarks than LSDM, particularly in large tropical and subtropical basins. For the SLR+GRACE reconstruction, median cKGE values are 0.59 for OS LISFLOOD and 0.50 for LSDM for detrended TWS, and 0.41 and 0.23, respectively, for interannual variability. More importantly, SLR+GRACE and SLR+DORIS yield the same sign of ΔNSE in 70.7% of cases for detrended TWS and 64.3% for interannual variability. The median absolute difference in ΔNSE between the two benchmarks increases from 0.12 to 0.20, indicating that model assessment is largely robust to benchmark choice, but becomes more sensitive at interannual timescales.In addition, degree-1 coefficients and the corresponding geocenter motion were reconstructed from the SLR+GRACE solution for 1995–2023. This extends the reconstructed geocenter series into the pre-GRACE era, fills the gap between GRACE and GRACE-FO, and complements our long-term gravity field reconstruction with degree-1 information.

items.title: Assimilation of GRACE/-FO data into global hydrological models for water use scenarios

items.text: Global Hydrological Models (GHMs) are an invaluable tool for simulating the dynamics of our freshwater cycle and estimating its contribution to sea level rise. However, uncertainties of input data (e.g., meteorological forcing, water demand estimates) and empirical parameters, as well as errors in the model structure (e.g., simplified representation through conceptual equations) lead to hydrological predictions that can vary strongly between different GHMs. Validation with independent satellite and in-situ observations shows that no single model can outperform the others in all regions and in all periods. Thus, assimilation of hydrological state variables into GHMs is a great opportunity to reduce model prediction uncertainty and improve performance statistics. Over the last two decades, the assimilation of terrestrial water storage (TWS) anomalies observed by the satellite gravity missions GRACE and GRACE-FO into land surface and water balance models has shown great potential to improve predictive capacity.In this presentation, we focus on exploiting the potential of TWS data assimilation into GHMs to reveal the human water use impact on shifts of TWS patterns under changing climate. We compare two decades of TWS simulated by the open-source and Python re-programmed WaterGAP Global Hydrology Model (WGHM) version while (a) disregarding and (b) considering surface water and groundwater extraction to isolate the human impact on the terrestrial water cycle. The identified patterns are compared to GRACE/-FO-derived TWS long-term trends to identify their correlation for regions with intense water use activities. This enables to map regions under acute and chronic water stress, where water overconsumption shows significant impact on shifting TWS patterns. In addition, we perform a global TWS data assimilation experiment into the World-Wide Water Resources Assessment (W3RA) model using the open-source Python-based Global Land Data Assimilation system (PyGLDA) developed by our research group. A comparison of the W3RA predictions before and after data assimilation reveals the spatial and temporal signatures that are introduced from GRACE/-FO observations. Comparisons to the isolated human impact on the terrestrial water cycle from WGHM simulations enables the generation of a global map displaying the potential of GRACE/-FO data for improved representation of human activities on the water cycle.

items.text: Changes in terrestrial water storage (TWS) can be observed globally by the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) mission, whereas microwave remote sensing primarily provides information on near-surface soil moisture. However, obtaining reliable information on water storage changes in deeper soil layers remains a challenge. A simple yet effective approach is the use of an exponential filter, which approximates deeper soil moisture by accounting for the delayed response to surface soil water variations. Yet, constraining these deeper storage dynamics at the global scale remains difficult. GRACE-derived TWS offers a global observational constraint on integrated subsurface water storage variations.This study utilises soil moisture products from the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative (ESA CCI), including both surface and root zone soil moisture, together with daily GRACE-derived TWS to assess the potential of GRACE for constraining exponential depth extrapolation of satellite soil moisture. Focusing on detrended, deseasonalised sub-seasonal signals, we compare the agreement between daily GRACE-derived TWS and exponentially filtered soil moisture for different soil moisture integration depths. This allows us to assess how well the observed and depth-extrapolated soil moisture dynamics represent sub-seasonal TWS variability and to identify regions where storage dynamics beyond the represented soil depth may be relevant. The results demonstrate the potential of GRACE as an observational constraint for depth-extrapolating satellite soil moisture and reveal spatial differences in the relevance of deeper subsurface storage dynamics.

items.text: Time-variable gravity data as derived from the GRACE and GRACE-FO satellite missions contain the superposition of various mass change signals such as terrestrial water storage or ice mass change, as well as strong correlated noise. A common strategy for extracting specific geophysical signals from the data is to apply de-noising filters such as the DDK or VDK filters for suppressing the noise, and subsequently reducing non-targeted signals using physical forward models. Since both of these steps introduce and propagate errors to the extracted geophysical target signal, we propose an alternative strategy using a deep learning algorithm.The method consists of two subsequent steps: In the first step, the neural network is trained to co-predict several gravity signal components and a noise component when given their sum. For this training step, realistic forward-modeled signal components given by the ESA Earth System Model and a numerically simulated noise component assuming a GRACE-type gravity mission are used. In the subsequent testing step, the trained algorithm is applied to real GRACE/-FO monthly anomalous gravity grids. The proposed pipeline covers both the de-noising and signal separation step, and thereby represents an alternative processing method for (unfiltered) Level-2B to Level-3 GRACE/-FO data processing. Comparing the achieved results to equivalent state-of-the-art GRACE/-FO Level-3 data products such as those provided by the GFZ GravIS portal shows the proposed method to be beneficial in terms of the de-noising performance, as well as the preservation of small-scale details in the estimated signals.

items.text: The GRACE/GRACE-FO mission has been monitoring monthly variations of the Earth’s gravity field for more than two decades. One source of error in the gravity field estimation process is the uncertainty of the satellites’ attitude. The errors of the attitude determination propagate to the inter-satellite range observations via the antenna offset centre (AOC) correction.Compared to GRACE, GRACE-FO carries an additional third star camera, which, together with the gyroscopes, usually makes attitude errors negligible. However, the current coarse pointing mode, employed to increase mission lifetime, enlarges the propagated attitude errors.As a next step, we aim to incorporate full covariances for the AOC correction into the stochastic model. For this purpose, this work conducts in-house level-1A attitude data processing, including sensor fusion of the star camera and gyroscope data, along with variance component estimation. The stochastic model of the star camera data is extended to account for spatial dependencies across the celestial sky, as well as for temporal correlations. The impact on the post-fit residuals and the quality of the recovered gravity field is analysed as part of the ITSG gravity field processing at the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology.

items.title: A traceable GRACE/GRACE-FO Level-1C scientific dataset (2002-2026) for reproducible mass-change analysis
items.authors: Fan Yang1, Yi Wu2, Maike Schumacher1, and Ehsan Forootan1

items.text: While monthly Level-2 products of GRACE/-FO are widely used as essential climate variables for mass-transport studies, published processing chains and intermediate outputs are often insufficiently documented for transparent diagnostics, method intercomparison, and fully reproducible re-solving. Building on existing uses of the Level-1C concept, we present Hawk Level-1C, an integrated scientific dataset that links calibrated Level-1B observations with monthly Level-2 gravity fields and supports consistent, transparent, traceable, and reproducible mass-change studies with GRACE/GRACE-FO. Specifically, this Level-1C dataset comprises four subsets: (1) K-band range-rate residuals, (2) line-of-sight gravity differences, (3) normal equations, and (4) calibrated accelerometer data. Each subset provides much complementary information beyond conventional Level-2 gravity fields and opens up new scientific applications, making it possible to (1) recover the submonthly gravity signal, (2) monitor rapidly evolving events such as floods and hurricanes, (3) enable accurate land water assimilation/fusion, and (4) perform neutral density modeling related to space weather. This product is provided on a monthly basis, spanning the available mission months from April 2002 to June 2026, to cover both GRACE and GRACE-FO, which will be openly available through Zenodo soon. In addition, we declare that this Level-1C, as well as the companion Level-2 product, is completely reproducible through our open source software and the configuration files provided. In this work, the entire data processing chain from Level-1B to Level-1C and Level-2 is documented. Long term diagnosis and rigorous validation of our Level-1C against other publicly available resources are carried out, which have demonstrated the satisfactory quality of our product. In the end, we showcase how this product helps to explore and exploit the scientific potential of GRACE/GRACE-FO in a manner different from the standard Level-2 product.

items.title: Benefits of future satellite gravimetry missions for characterizing extreme wet events in terrestrial water storage
items.authors: Klara Middendorf1, Laura Jensen2, Marius Schlaak3,4, Julian Haas2, Henryk Dobslaw2, Roland Pail3, Andreas Güntner2, and Annette Eicker1,2

items.text: Under the assumption that a warming climate leads to an intensification of the global water cycle, it is hypothesized that also the occurrence frequency and severity of extreme events such as droughts and floods will increase in the upcoming decades. GRACE/-FO observations of terrestrial water storage (TWS) have been used in the past to identify and analyse extreme events both on a global and regional scale. However, these analyses are restricted by the limited spatial and temporal resolution of current satellite gravimetry observations. Especially, flooding events tend to occur very locally and with short temporal (sub-monthly) extent, thus capturing them is challenging. Future satellite gravimetry missions, particularly the double-pair constellation MAGIC, are expected to significantly enhance the spatial and temporal resolution. In this study, we globally investigate the benefit MAGIC can achieve to detect wet extreme events using long-term (50 years) end-to-end simulations of GRACE-C and MAGIC.The simulation environment is based on the acceleration approach and considers tidal and non-tidal background model errors as well as instrument noise of the acceleration and ranging instruments following the current MAGIC mission design studies. As input and reference, we use the daily output of a climate model (GFDL-CM4) from the CMIP6 archive that has been identified as a realistic representation of water storage evolution in previous studies. To explore the improved temporal and spatial resolution expected from the MAGIC constellation, we (i) compare extreme values derived from 5-daily gravity field simulations to those from monthly fields, and (ii) show how the weaker spatial filtering required for MAGIC has a positive influence on the detectability of extremes.For the analysis two different approaches are exploited: One method focuses solely on the stochastic characteristics of the time series in terms of extreme value theory, evaluating the magnitude-frequency relationship of large TWS values by calculating expected return levels of wet extremes. The other approach builds on the fact that a 50-years simulation time series allows to derive statistically meaningful conclusions from directly comparing reference and simulation output on a time series level. We evaluate the time of occurrence of wet extremes on the basis of classification scores assessing correctly and incorrectly identified extreme events.

items.text: For 20 years now, GRACE and GRACE-FO data have been integrated into hydrological and land-surface models using data assimilation (DA) approaches. Numerous studies have demonstrated the value of GRACE/-FO DA systems for improving estimates of groundwater evolution, enhancing drought monitoring, and providing more accurate flood potential estimates. However, unlike other observation types such as remotely sensed soil moisture, GRACE/-FO observations are rarely assimilated into hydrological and land-surface models on an operational basis. With the prospect of near-real-time observations from upcoming satellite gravimetry missions, the question of how to make GRACE/-FO DA more broadly applicable is becoming increasingly relevant.Currently, there is no single established method for assimilating GRACE/-FO data into hydrological and land-surface models. While some settings have already reached a certain degree of consensus, for example suitable ensemble-based DA methods and the treatment of GRACE/-FO error covariance matrices, other aspects remain less well established. A key challenge is that GRACE/-FO observes integrated terrestrial water storage, whereas hydrological and land-surface models represent this storage through different components, such as soil moisture, snow, groundwater, and surface water. Assimilating GRACE/-FO data therefore requires determining how the observed TWS information is distributed among the model states. The formulation of the state vector and observation operator plays an important role in this process: the state vector determines which model variables are included in the assimilation, while the observation operator determines how these states are combined to represent the integrated TWS observed by GRACE/-FO. Different formulations of the state vector and observation operator can therefore change how information from the observations is distributed among storage components. Additionally, the representation of model uncertainty can strongly influence the assimilation results. We illustrate these challenges using two different DA systems: one based on the global model WaterGap Global Hydrological Model (WGHM) and one based on the regional high-resolution European land-surface model enCore Community Land Model (eCLM).Our results from eCLM-DA show that the choice of the state vector and the representation of model uncertainty strongly influence the assimilation results. Experiences with WGHM further indicate that some of these challenges are common across modelling systems, while others depend on model structure and resolution. We therefore distinguish between general methodological challenges, model-specific requirements, and computational and operational constraints, and identify areas where further methodological development is needed, including for coupled and multivariate DA systems. These considerations highlight challenges that must be overcome for the broader application of GRACE/-FO DA across modelling systems and regions, including its integration into regional monitoring and early warning systems.

items.text:
Temporal aliasing of sub-monthly gravimetric signals originating from the Earth's fluid envelope is a major source of error in time-variable gravity field models derived from the GRACE and GRACE Follow-On missions. Minimizing these errors to detect gravimetric signals providing information on solid Earth dynamics and the climate system remains a major challenge.
The GET and LEGOS laboratories in Toulouse have calculated the atmospheric and oceanic contributions to the time-variable gravity field, compiled into the OMP 2025 AOD1B dealiasing products, for the future processing of GRACE and GRACE-FO data.These products rely on an updated and improved version of the TUGO ocean dynamics numerical model and the ECMWF ERA5 3D atmosphere model. These atmospheric and oceanic dealiasing products (OMP 2025) include: (1) time-variable atmospheric gravitational potential anomalies generated from ECMWF ERA5 model levels (including hydrometeors, i.e., specific water content of rain, snow, cloud liquid, and ice), realistically distributed according to altitude above the geoid; and (2) time-variable oceanic gravitational potential anomalies calculated from ocean tides forced by ERA5 ocean surface fields (pressure and wind), with these water height anomalies realistically placed on the geoid. The oceanic response to atmospheric forcing is derived from the TUGO hydrodynamic model without assimilation and the FES2022 ocean tide model (validated by altimetry tides).These new dealiasing products are compared, after GRACE/GRACE-FO data reduction, meaning at the gravity field solution level, with the GFZ AOD1B RL06 and RL07 products officially used in GRACE/GRACE-FO processing. To this end, monthly GRACE gravity field solutions were calculated for 2006 and 2020 using these different dealiasing products, and the resulting monthly solutions are compared to analyze their differences. The analysis of post-fit residual differences between different dealiasing gravitational potential models, as well as the RMS of quiet zones and differences in monthly GRACE/-FO variable field solutions, will be presented.
Additionally, the new GFZ MIXED2025 ocean tide model is compared to the LEGOS FES2022 model at the gravity field solution level.

items.text: CNES has been producing solutions of the time-variable gravity field from GRACE and GRACE-FO data for many years. In addition to the unconstrained solutions — which along with many others are submitted to the COST-G international service to derive a combined monthly solution — CNES produces original stabilized solutions at monthly and 10-day time resolutions. These solutions thus differ from both unstabilized spherical harmonic solutions and mascon solutions.This presentation aims to detail the processes used to derive our solutions, specifically the singular value decomposition technique stabilized by a Tikhonov constraint, and the incorporation at the normal equations level of SLR data necessary for the accurate determination of low-degree terms. A comparison of the resulting solutions with spherical harmonic and mascon solutions will be presented. We will also outline efforts underway for a complete reprocessing of GRACE and GRACE-FO data, including the testing of new de-aliasing and ocean tide models, the fixing of GPS integer ambiguities, and the incorporation of instrument and geophysical model variance-covariance matrices required for data processing.

items.authors: Rebecca McGirr and Paul Tregoning

items.text: Currently available GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE(-FO)) mascon solutions differ due to variations in parameterization, regularization and land-ocean classification, leading to inconsistencies in regional mass change estimates. To reduce dependence on any single processing strategy, we present the first fused mascon solution, COM-TG, derived from four independent GRACE(-FO) products generated by separate analysis centers and combined within a consistent inversion framework. Prior to fusion, inconsistencies in land-ocean signal attribution were addressed using a coastline resolution improvement (CRI) approach. The fused solution is solved on $\sim0~km mascons delimited by coastlines and grounding lines, and is shown to be relatively insensitive to the choice of observation weighting used. It mitigates center-specific regularization assumptions, suppresses noise relative to individual input products and preserves meaningful spatial variability. The resulting product provides a unified representation of GRACE(-FO) mass changes for hydrological, oceanographic and cryospheric applications.

items.text: Ice mass loss in Greenland attracts considerable public attention because the Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS) is the largest single contributor to the mass component of global sea-level rise. To project the future evolution of the GrIS over the coming decades, accurate geophysical models are required. In particular, regional climate models, such as the Regional Atmospheric Climate Model RACMO2.3/RACMO2.3p2, are used to estimate the Surface Mass Balance (SMB) of the GrIS and surrounding areas. Data from the GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GFO) satellite gravity missions provide a primary source of independent information for evaluating modelled mass anomalies integrated over individual GrIS drainage systems and Greenland as a whole.In this study, we compare Greenland-wide estimates of annual mass trends derived from RACMO2.3/2.3p2 with those obtained from GRACE/GFO level-2 data for the period 2003–2023. As input, we use monthly sets of GRACE/GFO-based spherical harmonic coefficients produces at four institutions: the Center of Space Research (CSR) at the University of Texas at Austin; the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ) in Potsdam; the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) of the California Institute of Technology; and the Institute of Geodesy at Graz University of Technology (ITSG), Austria. The SMB-based estimates from RACMO2.3/2.3p2, combined with information on ice discharge (Mankoff et al, 2020), provide estimates of the total mass trends using the input-output method. We aim to ensure full consistency between the datasets being compared and their processing. Since the spatial resolution of RACMO model is substantially higher than that of GRACE/GFO data, we transform the RACMO-based mass anomalies into the spherical harmonic domain before further processing. In addition, we use fully consistent sets of months for both datasets to mitigate the potential impact of temporal gaps in GRACE/GFO data.The comparison conducted in this study allows us, first and foremost, to draw conclusions about the performance of RACMO2.3/2.3p2. For example, a recent study by Ran et al (Nature, 2024), based on elastic rock deformations measured by GPS during 2009–2015 showed that RACMO2.3p2 may underestimate meltwater runoff in “hot” years and overestimate it in “cold” years. By considering a substantially longer time interval, our study provides an independent evaluation of meltwater runoff modelled by RACMO2.3/2.3p2. At the same time, comparing GRACE/GFO-based estimates from different data processing centres with RACMO-based estimates enables us to assess the accuracy of the considered GRACE/GFO data products in the context of Greenland.

items.text:
Within the framework of the Research Unit NEROGRAV (New Refined Observations of Climate Change from Spaceborne Gravity Missions), we focus on the computation of daily gravity field solutions using a Kalman filter approach. We use the RL07p GRACE/GRACE-FO daily normal equations, which incorporate refined stochastic modeling of the observations and background models. The stochastic information on the geophysical processes governing submonthly gravity field variations is derived from HISerr time series.
In this study, we present GFZ daily gravity field solutions for the five-year period from 2004 to 2008. To investigate the impact of different processing strategies, several Kalman filter configurations are tested. These include the use of different a priori gravity field models, different approaches to constructing the required hydrological variance-covariance matrix, and the application of a Kalman smoother in comparison with the corresponding raw Kalman filter solutions. The resulting solutions are assessed in terms of their consistency and sensitivity to the different processing choices.
Validation is performed in two ways. First, the GFZ daily solutions are compared with independent daily Kalman filter solutions computed at TU Graz. Second, the daily gravity field solutions are evaluated by comparison with the vertical components of GNSS stations from the global IGS network. This provides an external assessment of the temporal variations captured by the daily gravity field solutions.

items.text: We introduce a daily and 25-km spatiotemporally downscaled GRACE/-FO Terrestrial Water Storage Anomaly (TWSA) dataset for the Contiguous United States (CONUS) spanning 2002–2024. To address the resolution gap between coarse monthly satellite observations and daily hydrometeorological dynamics, we developed a physics-informed Dual-Stream Deep Learning (DL) architecture. The framework synchronously trains a monthly physics-constrained estimator by enforcing strict mass conservation via a global mass budget projection and a daily probabilistic estimator that models conditional predictive distributions using a Student-t likelihood to accommodate heavy-tailed GRACE/-FO TWSA residuals. Internal validation demonstrates that the downscaled product preserves the long-term trends and spatial variance of the native GRACE/-FO observations while outperforming standard land surface models that are used as input of DL framework. Crucially, the daily temporal resolution enables the quantification of high-frequency hydrologic extremes that are typically obscured in monthly gravity fields. We extensively validated the daily TWSA dataset against a 22-year catalog of Atmospheric River (AR) events in California and 104 different Tropical Cyclone (TC) events across the eastern CONUS. The downscaled TWSA successfully resolves rapid mass loading with a near-zero phase lag relative to independent in-situ streamflow and precipitation networks. The resulting simulation yields a mass-conserving, physically interpretable daily TWSA product suitable for high-frequency hydrological and climate applications.

items.text: Specific yield (Sy) is a fundamental hydrogeological parameter governing groundwater storage and availability in unconfined aquifers. However, its estimation at regional to continental scales remains challenging because of the limited availability of reliable in-situ observations. Existing estimates commonly rely on hydrogeological maps or model-calibrated values, which may involve substantial uncertainties and often do not adequately represent spatial variability. Here, we develop an observation-based framework to estimate spatially varying Sy across India by integrating seasonal in-situ groundwater-level observations with groundwater storage changes derived from GRACE/GRACE-FO observations using the water table fluctuation method. Sy was estimated at the GRACE mascon scale (~3°) for 2003–2022, providing a consistent assessment of regional variability across India. The estimated Sy exhibits distinct spatial patterns, with relatively higher values across north-eastern and parts of peninsular India and lower values across western India. Comparison with reference Sy derived from hydrogeological information shows generally good agreement across several mascons, while differences in selected regions highlight spatial heterogeneity that may not be adequately represented by map-based estimates. Uncertainty analysis based on error propagation indicates that the estimated Sy values largely fall within the uncertainty ranges of the reference estimates. To assess the influence of spatial resolution, Sy was additionally estimated using a downscaled GRACE/GRACE-FO groundwater storage product at 0.5° resolution. The downscaled product provides negligible improvement over the mascon-scale estimates, demonstrating that the GRACE mascon framework is adequate for regional to continental scale Sy estimation. The proposed framework provides an observation constrained approach for characterizing spatial variability in Sy and can support large-scale assessments of groundwater storage and availability. Nevertheless, the estimates remain constrained by the spatial resolution of GRACE observations and the temporal and spatial coverage of groundwater-level measurements, limiting their applicability for local-scale aquifer characterization.

items.text: Observational and modelled components of the continental water cycle still show considerable variation between available data products. At the same time, however, the research community is trying to identify processes and changes across several domains of the hydrosphere in increasingly more detail.Within the Collaborative Research Centre (CRC) 1502 DETECT, we have developed an analysisframework in order to assess the mass budget consistency of observational and modelled water flux products. We evaluate essential climate variables such as precipitation (P), evaporation from land (E), terrestrial water storage (TWS) change (dTWS/dt), and river discharge (Q) by means of kernel-integrated monthly water mass fluxes in the GRACE/-FO era. Specifically, we focus on the terrestrial water balance equation as in dTWS/dt+Q=P−E, which states that net flux P−E between atmosphere and surface must be balanced by the combination of dTWS/dt and Q.In our major assessment 2003-01/2022-12 over the EURO-CORDEX region, we assessed budget flux components for 30+ major river catchments, including a wide selection of observational and reanalysis products, such as e.g. GPCC, MSWEP, ERA5, GLEAM, GRDC and COST-G (and other GRACE-related products). While individual data products can vary considerably on a per-month basis and in their relative offsets, we find that clear majority (~74%) of catchments show drying P−E behaviour, while the balance-term dTWS/dt+Q shows mostly consistent behaviour (~67%). Notably, out of the basins with a maximum P−E net flux of +25 mm/month, >90% show drying trends in P−E, and >85% show negative trends in the combination of TWS change and river discharge.While dP/dt, across Europe, is heterogeneously distributed spatially and across data products, E more consistently increased by 1 mm/month per decade. On average, TWS losses increased and discharge declined. In contrast to absolute fluxes, dTWS/dt+Q change appears, on average, ~equally caused by a decline in discharge and TWS; the trends, however, exhibit large uncertainties. In total, a flux budget misclosure remains below 2 mm/month.We again point out that researchers must be aware of the notable variability between available data products and avoid 'cherry-picking' of analysis products.

items.authors: Malte Greuner, Joshua Reeder, Max Rohr, and Koch Alexander

affiliations.text: DLR Institute for Satellite Geodesy and Inertial Sensing, Hannover, Germany DLR Institute for Satellite Geodesy and Inertial Sensing, Hannover, Germany

items.text: Today’s best laser-ranging instruments, such as those on GRACE-FO, GRACE-C and NGGM, reach nanometer-level precision, or have their sensing noise requirement on that level. However, they are large, expensive, and designed for big satellites. The costs for such GRACE-like missions exceed M€ 500, and their gravity fields are usually provided on a monthly level, which is too slow for many hydrologic processes. The MAGIC constellation attempts to increase the temporal resolution, but is limited to ~weekly products. To observe rapid water changes and aid, e.g., in flood-prediction, increased ground-track coverage is required. A cost-effective way to achieve this is with pairs of SmallSats in different orbital planes, carrying compact and comparably cheap payloads.This is the motivation for the miniaturisation of a laser-interferometric ranging payload for SmallSat constellations, with a target size below 8 U, weight below 6 kg and power below 20 W. It seeks ranging precision better than 1 µm/√Hz × NSF(f) between 10⁻³ and 10⁻¹ Hz.Instead of using a large optical reference cavity, our miniature LRI will use modulation transfer spectroscopy with a rubidium molecular reference and a 780 nm external-cavity diode laser. The same laser system could be used in a future implementation for a Rb-based accelerometer. The instrument also uses an on-axis optical bench layout to avoid the triple-mirror assembly, and adds satellite communication over the same laser link, enabling data transfer between the two spacecraft, as well as absolute ranging at the centimeter-level.In this presentation, we will report on the design, currently on-going laboratory tests of key enablers for such an instrument as well as the next steps towards the implementation of an Engineering Model. In short, a SmallSat inter-satellite ranging payload turns proven gravity-measurement ideas into a SmallSat-compatible, quantum-aligned payload that could make frequent, low-cost Earth Observation possible - and may later support planetary missions such as the MaQuIs mission around Mars.

items.authors: Tyler Sutterley1 and Isabella Velicogna2,3

affiliations.text: University of Washington, Applied Physics Laboratory, Polar Science Center, Seattle, United States of America

items.text: We look to understand how uncertainties in atmospheric pressure affect the precision of Antarctic ice sheet mass balance estimates derived from time-variable gravity measurements using an ensemble of reanalysis outputs along with in-situ observations of surface pressure. Before the formulation of monthly spherical harmonic gravitational fields from GRACE and GRACE Follow-On, sub-monthly atmospheric variations are removed using the "de-aliasing" products computed from ERA reanalyses and ECMWF operational forecasts and processed by the German Research Centre for Geosciences (GFZ). While this helps remove the majority of the atmospheric signal globally, the quality of atmospheric forecasts and analyses is typically lower over Antarctica due to the scarcity of available data and the strong topographic contrasts. As uncertainties in the dealiasing fields directly map into errors in the spherical harmonic fields, improving the characterization of atmospheric circulation over the poles will help improve the month-by-month precision of Antarctic mass change estimates. Here, we estimate the impacts of atmospheric pressure uncertainty on ice sheet mass balance at both continental and regional scales using four independently derived reanalyses (ERA5, MERRA-2, JRA-3Q, and NCEP-CFSR). We find that equivalent atmospheric pressure uncertainties of 1 millibar over the entirety of Antarctica will result in a mass uncertainty of over 100 gigatonnes. From our reanalysis ensemble, we find average monthly uncertainties of 0.6–1.1 millibars (71–132 gigatonnes) over the continent, likely limiting our present-day mass change estimates over short timescales. Additionally, we calculate the atmospheric loading effects in Antarctica under different scenarios related to the structure of the Earth's atmosphere and Earth's geometry. We find that for the purposes of deriving atmospheric pressure uncertainties, simple two-dimensional formulations are likely adequate.

items.text: The Gravitational Reference Advanced Technology Test In Space (GRATTIS) mission will demonstrate the functionality and sensitivity performance of the Simplified Gravitational Reference Sensor (S-GRS), an ultra-precise inertial sensor for future Earth geodesy missions. These sensors are used to measure or compensate for all non-gravitational accelerations of the host spacecraft so that they can be removed in the data analysis to recover spacecraft motion due to Earth’s gravity field. Low-low satellite-to-satellite tracking missions like GRACE-FO that utilize laser ranging are technologically limited by the acceleration noise performance of their accelerometers, as well as temporal aliasing associated with Earth’s dynamic gravity field.The S-GRS concept is a simplified version of the LISA Pathfinder GRS. It consists of a free-falling cubic test mass (TM) inside an electrode housing that senses the position and orientation of the TM and electrostatically applies forces and torques to keep it centered at a nanometer-level. The applied forces and torques required are also used to determine the non-gravitational forces acting on the host spacecraft, as well as the spacecraft’s angular acceleration. Improvements incorporated into the S-GRS include removing the small grounding wire used in the GRACE accelerometers, which limits performance, and replacing it with a UV LED-based charge management system, increasing the mass of the sensor’s TM, and increasing the gap between the TM and its electrode housing.GRATTIS will fly two identical S-GRS mounted next to one another near the center of mass of a 235 kg ESPA-class commercial microsatellite. The six-axis acceleration measurement capability of the S-GRS allows precision measurement of the spacecraft drag-induced translational acceleration, as well as the residual angular acceleration of the nominally inertially-pointed bus. By combining the outputs of each sensor and with the known relative position of the two TMs, we can recover the acceleration sensitivity (noise floor) of the S-GRS. Our mission goal is to demonstrate acceleration noise performance of ≤10–10 m/s2Hz1/2.The PI and science team is led by the University of Florida (UF) and includes relevant experts from Texas A&M University (TAMU) and CrossTrac Engineering. The S-GRS mechanical sensor heads are provided by BAE Space & Mission Systems, while the S-GRS electronics units are provided by Fibertek, Inc. CrossTrac Engineering provides the S-GRS software and program management. The flight S-GRS payload has been integrated and tested at the University of Florida in August-September 2026. The payload was then delivered to the spacecraft provider (Apex Space) and is in the final stages of integration and test with the spacecraft. The integrated spacecraft will be delivered to SpaceX in late 2026 for integration with the launch vehicle. GRATTIS is manifested on SpaceX Transporter-19 launching from Vandenburg Space Force Base into a 561 km sun-synchronous orbit no earlier than February 1, 2027. This presentation will describe the GRATIS technology demonstration mission, current status, and expected results.
