items.title: Mantle Rheology Across Tidal to Decadal Timescales
items.authors: Lambert Caron, Erik Ivins, Surendra Adhikari, and Erin Hightower

affiliations.text: Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology

items.text: Long-period deformation of the solid Earth provides a unique window into mantle rheology between seismic and glacial-isostatic-adjustment (GIA) timescales, where constitutive behavior remains poorly constrained. Laboratory experiments increasingly support broad transient anelastic relaxation, while geodynamic studies disfavor the extremely low steady-state viscosities that would otherwise be required to explain some long-period observations. The Extended Burgers Material (EBM) offers a linear viscoelastic framework that captures this transient relaxation while asymptotically approaching Maxwell behavior at long timescales.Using newly developed Love-number capabilities in the Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (ISSM), we compile and model complex degree-2 tidal Love-number constraints k, h, and l from satellite laser ranging, satellite gravity, Earth-rotation observations, GNSS, and DORIS over periods from 12 hours to 18.6 years. We first test whether the observations can be explained by radial steady-state viscosity structure alone using a large ensemble of flexible layered Maxwell models. These models reproduce much of the gravitational and radial response, but systematically fail to reproduce the real horizontal response, even when very low viscosities are permitted in the lowermost mantle or introduced in the transition zone and asthenosphere.We then explore EBM rheologies with distinct upper- and lower-mantle properties. These models reproduce the joint frequency dependence of Love numbers significantly better while retaining steady-state viscosities compatible with GIA constraints. The results point to an important role for transient lower-mantle relaxation, although correlations between relaxation amplitude and timescale, and the long-period cutoff of the transient response, remain incompletely resolved. Better constraints on this behavior are directly relevant to GRACE and GRACE-FO, as well as GNSS, SLR, DORIS, altimetry, and other remote-sensing observations that depend on accurate modeling of solid-Earth deformation across overlapping timescales.© 2026 California Institute of Technology. items.authors: Shin-Chan Han1 and George Pescod2,1

items.text: The attitude of the GRACE Follow-On satellites is controlled by six pairs of attitude control thrusters. An ideal thruster system would produce a change only in angular momentum. The imperfect system, however, also produces undesired linear accelerations that must be removed for orbit analysis and gravity recovery. On-orbit calibration is performed to determine the linear acceleration response to each of the six thrust events for both satellites. These thrust calibration models are applied to the ACC1B data product and its variants. As is standard for L1B data products, a CRN low-pass filter is applied with a cutoff frequency of 35 mHz for the case of the ACC1B datasets. This cutoff frequency was chosen for orbit and gravity analysis using KBR1B from the beginning of the GRACE mission, considering the balance between dampening gravitational signals and increasing KBR thermal noises with frequency. We found spurious acceleration signals, most clearly visible in the form of range acceleration computed from LRI1B data and a prefit dynamic orbit. These spurious accelerations were in fact LRI measurements of thrust events — all six cases — appearing in a frequency band well above 35 mHz. We discuss how the LRI measures thruster firings, how we model and remove them, and why this modeling matters for global gravity recovery.

items.text: Human activities are reshaping Earth’s freshwater stores, but the spatial resolution of satellite gravimetry has limited its utility in resolving these changes at scales relevant to water management. Here we use a “stacked” regression of 23 years of GRACE and GRACE Follow-On Level-1B intersatellite range observations to map global terrestrial water storage (TWS) trends at finer spatial resolution than conventional monthly mascon products. The resulting trend map resolves features at approximately 12,500 km² and retains substantially more of the underlying mass signal. We combine this spatially refined solution with uncertainty analysis, spatial statistical methods, and independent datasets describing land and water use, climate variability, and glacier mass loss, to investigate the drivers of observed TWS trends. We identify 40 regions where TWS trends are significantly associated with anthropogenic activities, including groundwater and surface-water irrigation, rainfed agriculture, deforestation, and reservoir impoundment. Regional TWS trend magnitudes are, on average, larger than those derived from conventional monthly mascon products and those reported in previous studies, particularly in over-exploited aquifers. The higher-resolution solution also reveals that localized freshwater gains associated with rainfed agriculture, surface-water irrigation, and reservoir filling, and losses from groundwater pumping and agriculture, are globally pervasive, with anthropogenic independent variables explaining a significant portion of TWS trend spatial variability in every non-polar continent except Australia. These results provide a detailed picture of global mass change and demonstrate the potential of improved satellite gravimetry processing to reveal human influences on freshwater storage.

items.text: GRACE-Continuity (GRACE-C) is a joint NASA (US) & DLR (Germany) mission, scheduled for launch in Dec-2028. It will continue the essential data record of Earth system gravity and mass change initiated by the original GRACE mission (2002-2017) and currently enabled by the GRACE-FO mission (2018 – present). The GRACE-series provides foundational observations of monthly to decadal global mass changes and transports in the Earth system derived from temporal variations in the Earth’s gravity field. These data are indispensable for accurately measuring the evolving global water cycle, including ocean dynamics, polar ice mass changes, and near-surface and global ground water changes. Mass Change data enable the monitoring of flood potentials as well as droughts by tracking freshwater availability, groundwater and aquifer volume changes. These observations and integrated tools built around them have become indispensable for 'water intelligence' to inform data-driven water-management.We will present an update on the implementation status of GRACE-C: the mission is well into its assembly, integration and testing phase. Key science instruments like the laser ranging interferometers, accelerometers, GNSS-receivers and star cameras are undergoing testing, and are being integrated on the two GRACE-C satellites. The GRACE-C SDS team is continuously assessing and verifying the measurement system performance throughout the flight system integration phase. The mission is on schedule to launch in late 2028. We will provide an assessment of the expected science performance, as well as plans for low- and high-level data products and algorithms to support optimal science and application mission return.

items.text:
The Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (GRACE-FO), launched in May 2018, provides invaluable information about mass change in the Earth system, continuing the legacy of GRACE. Fundamental requirements for successful mass change recovery are precise orbit determination and inter-satellite ranging, determination of the relative clock alignment of the ultra-stable oscillators (USOs), precise attitude determination, and accelerometry. NASA/Caltech Jet Propulsion Laboratory is the official Level-1 data processing and analysis center and provides weekly Level-1A/B data updates. Here we present analysis of the aforementioned GRACE-FO sensor data, status of the accelerometer transplant calibrations, as the basis for Level-2 release RL06.3, and a discussion of the overall GRACE-FO measurement system performance through Solar cycle 25. We also provide an update on current GRACE/GRACE-FO reprocessing efforts toward a future unified Release-07 data record.

items.text: GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) satellite observations provide a unique capability for quantifying long-term changes in terrestrial water storage and assessing groundwater depletion across large river basins where in situ observations are spatially limited or inconsistent. Here, we use GRACE/GRACE-FO observations together with land surface models, reservoir storage records, and water-use information to evaluate freshwater storage changes and their partitioning in two major transboundary river systems of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico: the Colorado River Basin and the Rio Grande-Bravo Basin.GRACE/GRACE-FO observations reveal persistent long-term water storage declines across both basins, with groundwater depletion representing a major component of the observed losses. In the Colorado River Basin, total water storage declined by 52.2 km³, with groundwater accounting for approximately 65% of the total loss, indicating that groundwater depletion has exceeded surface reservoir declines as the dominant source of freshwater loss. In the Rio Grande-Bravo Basin, groundwater depletion averages 2.7 km³ yr⁻¹, while 52% of direct anthropogenic water consumption is unsustainable and irrigated agriculture accounts for 87% of direct consumptive use. These results demonstrate the increasing reliance on groundwater to compensate for declining renewable surface-water supplies.The analysis highlights the value of GRACE/GRACE-FO for interpreting long-term hydrological trends and separating groundwater storage changes from other terrestrial water storage components. Combining satellite gravimetry with complementary hydrological datasets provides a consistent framework for evaluating basin-scale freshwater storage variations, identifying regions of persistent groundwater depletion, and improving understanding of the processes driving water storage decline in heavily managed and water-stressed river basins.

items.text:
The Atmosphere and Ocean non-tidal De-aliasing Level-1B (AOD1B) product is widely used in satellite gravimetry to correct for transient effects of atmosphere-ocean mass variability that would otherwise alias into monthly-mean global gravity fields. The most recent release is based on the global ERA5 reanalysis and ECMWF operational data together with simulations from the general ocean circulation model MPIOM consistently forced with fields of the same atmospheric data-set.
In this presentation we give a short overview of the current production status of AOD1B as well as current and future work on hydrological de-aliasing datasets.

items.text:
Over nearly 25 years, GRACE and GRACE-FO have matured from a novel observing system into an operational-grade data source, with terrestrial water storage anomaly (TWSA) and, derived from this, groundwater storage change (GWSC) products now feeding directly into drought, flood, and water-availability assessments. Despite this maturity, systematic translation of GRACE-based TWSA and GWSC into a sustained, standards-compliant climate service has so far been missing. This gap has limited uptake by climate adaptation and water-management communities which rely on Essential Climate Variable (ECV)-type products with defined uncertainty and provenance.
In this contribution, we present the operationalisation of GRACE-based hydrological science into a climate service through the introduction of a new Essential Climate Variable (ECV) Service, “Terrestrial Water Storage and Groundwater”, within the Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S). The service delivers Climate Data Records (CDRs) for TWSA and GWSC, built to C3S CDR requirements for homogeneity, traceability, and long-term consistency. The datasets, together with a comprehensive Data Documentation Package following C3S standards, are published on the Climate Data Store (CDS).
A key challenge in this operationalisation is quality characterisation in the near-absence of suitable in-situ reference data at GRACE's native spatial and temporal resolution. We address this with a dedicated quality assessment framework combining internal consistency checks (e.g., mass conservation, basin-scale closure), inter-comparison with global hydrological models and land-surface/reanalysis products, and the explicit documentation of known limitations and fitness-for-purpose. Additionally, TWSA is compared against independent mascon and spherical-harmonic solutions and GWSC against regionalised in-situ measurements from groundwater boreholes.
As the C3S strives towards more accessible information for the public and decision makers, both products contribute to Climate Intelligence efforts through a variety of visualisations across different time scales, which will also be presented here.

items.text: We present the GRACE and GRACE-FO Level-2 and Level-3 products generated at CSR, evaluating their quality using standard metrics. We also report on the RL07 reprocessing of GRACE and GRACE-FO data, which incorporates updated Level-1B observations, reference frames, background models, instrument calibrations, and processing strategies. New CSR mascon solutions are being developed within the same RL07 framework. The RL07 solutions reduce the RMS of the noise over the ocean by more than 35% compared to RL06.3, improving solution stability and the effective spatial resolution of mass-change estimates.

items.text:
Since 2018, the GRACE Follow-On satellite mission, a partnership between NASA (US) and GFZ (Germany), is continuing the unique essential climate data record of mass change in the Earth system initiated in 2002 by the GRACE mission (2002-2017). The combined GRACE & GRACE-FO data records now span over 22 years and provide foundational observations of monthly to decadal global mass changes and transports in the Earth system derived from temporal variations in the Earth’s gravity field. These observations have become indispensable for climate-related studies that enable process understanding of the evolving global water cycle, including ocean dynamics, polar ice mass changes, and near-surface and global ground water changes.

We will present recent GRACE/GRACE-FO science and applications highlights, status of the data processing, calibration approaches, performance of last year’s science data, and discuss the GRACE-FO mission operations plan to collect and provide high-quality science data, aiming for overlap with the upcoming NASA/DLR GRACE-Continuity mission, targeted to launch in late 2028.
